Снова горы донесений - кипа за кипой, отовсюду, со всех концов Союза. И в каждом - одно и то же: солдаты отказывались стрелять в бунтовщиков, офицеры дезертировали целыми взводами. Военная машина Иберии дышала на ладан.

Из-за стен кабинета Франко доносился многоголосый вой протестующих - оркестр проклятий под аккомпанемент полицейских сирен и далёкого гула вертолёта. Хаос у самого порога, но Франко не чувствовал ровно ничего. Муссолини спустил бы на них свору псов, Гитлер, не мешкая, открыл бы огонь. А он, чей кабинет заполнялся отдалёнными криками, бессильно читал о том, как прежние верные соратники покидают его один за другим.

Почти забавно, если подумать, что Салазару не довелось увидеть всего этого. Ему выпала мирная кончина до того, как нагрянул хаос. До того, как рухнуло всё, чему они посвятили свою жизнь. Франко отложил последнее донесение - всю стопку уже было не перечитать, да и незачем. Он признал правду. Ему суждено было стать свидетелем конца. Усталый взгляд скользил по стенам, пока до него доходило осознание.

Он не был застигнут врасплох. В этой буре не было ничего неожиданного. Мятежи, бунты, кровь - всё это лишь очередная глава в бесконечной книге европейской смуты, где прогресс растлевает души праведников. Люди бунтуют, сражаются, гибнут - так было и так будет всегда. Испании нужен не народ. Испании нужен Франко. Тот, кто однажды уже спас её от социалистического безумия. Тот, кто готов сделать это снова. Ничего особенного. Никаких фанфар. За окнами стонет Иберия - но стонет лишь оттого, что ищет твёрдой руки.

options.name: Каудильо поправил галстук. Сирены за окном выли, но он не обращал на них внимания.

title: Упорядоченный отход
desc:
Над Хаэном разгорался рассвет - небо полыхало оранжевым и багряным цветом, перетекавшим в синеву. В этот день бесценные сокровища семьи Франко должны были покинуть город и отправиться за океан, туда, где грозивший поглотить Испанию хаос не мог до них добраться. У ворот поместья стояли Кристобаль Мартинес-Бордиу и Николас Франко, распоряжаясь погрузкой картин в бронированные фургоны. Оба следили, как рабочие снуют туда-сюда, бережно укладывая драгоценный груз.

Николас потёр подбородок и вздохнул: "Подумать только - эти реликвии воплощают почти полвека власти и влияния. А теперь мы тайком вывозим их за океан. Право слово, это почти оскорбительно."

Кристобаль фыркнул: "А ты бы предпочёл оставить их здесь? Чтобы всё это растащили и разбили в щепки озверевшие толпы?" - он скрестил руки и мотнул головой. - "В Южной Америке им ничто не грозит. А когда Франсиско вернёт Иберию под свой контроль..." - усмехнулся он, обернувшись к Николасу. - "...мы вернём их обратно. На законное место."

Николас пожал плечами, провожая взглядом первые отъезжавшие от ворот фургоны: "А как же реформисты, Кристобаль? Они твердят, что переговоры всё ещё возможны. Может, войны и не будет вовсе."

Кристобаль рассмеялся - громко, искренне, и Николас нахмурился. Вздохнув, тот взял его за плечо и повёл обратно к дому: "Если бы всё зависело от них - они бы распродали половину Испании, после чего, довольные, забились бы обратно в свои норы. В их замыслах нет ни капли чести. Одна только трусость."

Николас опустил глаза и молча кивнул. А затем тихо спросил: "И всё же - очередная война. Стоит ли она того?" - Кристобаль цокнул, уже у самых дверей поместья повернувшись к нему на каблуках.

options.name: "Идеалы на войне гибнут первыми, Николас. Запомни это."

title: Фасад
desc:
Франсиско Франко Сальгадо-Араухо, двоюродной брат каудильо, сидел у дверей зала заседаний, нервно ворочаясь в кресле и машинально проводил подошвами по красному ковру. Рядом, за столиком, сидела секретарша, монотонно щёлкая клавишами своей печатной машинки - но даже этот стук почти не заглушал гневных выкриков, то и дело доносившихся из-за двери. Кузен был явно не в духе. Да и как ему быть в духе, когда на полуострове творится такое? Иберия не видела подобных потрясений со времён Гражданской войны, а Франсиско всё сильнее опасался, что его родина катится к той же пропасти, что в тридцатые. Нет. Он боялся, что в этот раз всё будет ещё хуже. Гораздо хуже.

Внезапно дверь распахнулась. На пороге возник офицер - его лицо было усталым, всё в морщинах и складках, взгляд потухший. Он молча поплёлся к выходу, и секретарша, кивнув, бросила: "Можете проходить, сеньор". Франсиско поднялся и переступил порог. За длинным столом, в дальнем конце комнаты, сидел его кузен.

Сальгадо-Араухо вскинул руку в салюте: "Ваше превосходительство." - Франко, мокрый от пота, с воспалёнными, красными глазами, коротко махнул, приглашая его сесть. За столом находились ещё семеро - все при орденах, все напряжённые, как струна. Сам Франко выглядел растерзанным: он покачивался на стуле, окидывал комнату бессмысленным взглядом и тяжело, надрывно вздыхал.

"У меня есть регулярная связь только с пятнадцатью офицерами с португальского фронта." - процедил каудильо сквозь зубы, прищурившись. - "Пятнадцать - из сотни штабных."

Горький, хриплый смешок сорвался с его губ, но тут же перешёл в затяжной приступ кашля, сотрясший всё его тело. Двоюродной брат невольно поморщился; остальные офицеры сидели недвижимо, будто каменные. Наконец кашель стих, и Франко выдохнул, с трудом переводя дыхание. - "Прошу прощения," - выдавил он, прочистил горло и повернулся к кузену. - "Ты как? Справляешься?"

Франсиско нахмурился, заёрзал на стуле и вместо ответа спросил: "А ты?"

options.name: Долго ли он ещё продержится?

title: Потерять свой дом
desc:
Едва ли не всю свою долгую власть над Иберией Франко мог положиться на десятки офицеров - они были при нём и в дни мира, и в дни смуты, готовые прийти на помощь и в делах государства, и в военных распрях. Так было когда-то. Но хаос, охвативший полуостров, не пощадил и его штаб; с каждым днём тех, кто ещё поднимал трубку, когда звонил каудильо, становилось всё меньше. Франко недоумевал, почему всё так сложилось, хотя в глубине души уже знал ответ - по какой причине на самом деле они не могли или не хотели ему отвечать.

Невесёлые мысли прервал стук в дверь кабинета: "Войдите," - бросил Франко. В комнату вошёл слегка растрёпанный адъютант и остановился у порога - взгляд в пол, ни единого шанса встретиться глазами с каудильо.

"Ваше превосходительство, боюсь..." - он замялся, прикусил губу. Франко повернулся к нему, насторожившись. - "Галисийские власти отказались признавать вашу власть над их землями. Час назад мы приняли их декларацию о независимости. Они объявили республику..."

Кулак Франко обрушился на стол. Красное дерево глухо вздрогнуло, и адъютант умолк на полуслове. В комнате повисла звенящая тишина - только дыхание каудильо, прерывистое и тяжёлое. Затем - долгий, глубокий выдох: "Благодарю. Вы... вы можете идти." - адъютант поспешно исчез за дверью, оставив Франко одного. Наедине с тем, что осталось от его мыслей.

Галисия была его домом. Его детство в Ферроле - солёный ветер с моря, зелёные холмы, бескрайние поля и луга - всё ещё жило в памяти, почти осязаемое. Теперь всё это ускользнуло, просочилось сквозь пальцы. Он подвёл свой народ. Он предал свою родину. Франко опустил голову, и на него упал косой луч закатного солнца, пробившийся сквозь высокое окно.

options.name: Он закрыл глаза, тоскуя по дому...
...пока воздух в Галисии звенел свободой.

title: По частям
desc:
Гостиная, некогда блиставшая роскошью, теперь казалась унылой и убогой - ни единой безделушки, ни одной вещицы, что могла бы напомнить о былом великолепии. Со стен исчезли бесценные полотна XVI века и парадные клинки, что висели там сотни лет. Не осталось ни старинной мебели, ни серебряных приборов, ни мавританских ковров. Кармен Поло бросила короткий взгляд в окно: люди грузили последние ящики в бронированные автомобили. Всё. Богатство Франко было спасено. И от этого она должна была испытать облегчение... но её мысли витали далеко отсюда. Как и остальные, она прислушивалась к голосу из радиоприёмника, который второпях принёс один из их людей.

Когда последние слова Торкуато Фернандеса-Миранды потонули в громе аплодисментов, Николас Франко щёлкнул тумблером радио, оборвав ликование севильян и погрузив гостиную в гнетущее молчание. Четверо в комнате не решались нарушить его - каждому требовалась минута, чтобы осознать услышанное.

Испанская Республика. Эти слова бились в висках, не желая затихать. Это уже была не борьба сепаратистов за независимость - на сей раз мятежники требовали полного крушения мадридского правительства. Реформисты отвернулись от них, а к ним присоединились и множество недовольных офицеров. Это была не простая горстка смутьянов в одной лишь Севилье - вся южная Испания ускользнула из их рук. Теперь больше половины страны подняла против них оружие: "Мне нужно увидеть Франсиско. Немедленно." - бросил Николас, прошагав мимо всех к двери. Кристобаль и её дочь последовали за ним, оставив Кармен наедине с собственными мыслями.

Сначала баски, потом португальцы, каталонцы, Марокко и Галисия, а теперь... что у них осталось? Она в последний раз взглянула в окно, провожая взглядом последние частицы их былой жизни. И на мгновение ей показалось, что она сама так же обнажена и беззащитна, как голые стены вокруг.

options.name: Дорога обратно в Мадрид была столь же безмолвной...
...пока голоса на юге становились всё громче.

title: Освобождён от обязанностей
desc:
Свет резал глаза. Беспощадные люминесцентные лампы заливали комнату мертвенно-белым сиянием, грозясь стереть в этой пустоте очертания стоявших напротив офицеров. Рядом с Франко застыли его близкие - отчуждённые, будто сами не до конца понимая, зачем они здесь, - и те немногие министры, что ещё от него не отвернулись. Все они теснились в тесном, запущенном кабинете на окраине Мадрида. Люди за столом вызвали его сюда. Отдали приказ. Он так и не понял что заставило его подчиниться - то ли остатки былой гордости, то ли последнее чувство долга.

"Ваше превосходительство," - Карлос Иньеста Кано слегка склонил голову. За ним последовал и его узкий круг соратников. Семья каудильо рассаживалась за круглый, сколоченный на скорую руку стол. Франко и Кано сели друг против друга, буравя друг друга взглядами: "Как вы, несомненно, заметили, гражданское управление Иберией больше невозможно. Государство захлестнули угрозы слишком серьёзные и слишком слаженные, чтобы обычные власти могли с ними справиться." - Франко сжал губы. Он знал, чем это кончится. Он понял это по улыбке Кано ещё в тот самый миг, когда в Севилье прозвучала прокламация об образовании Республики.

Генерал сложил руки на столе, выпрямился, не сводя с каудильо глаз: "В связи с этим я снимаю с федерального правительства Иберии все полномочия. Отныне власть переходит к временной военной администрации." - Он обернулся к охраннику и коротко кивнул. Тот трижды стукнул в дверь, и в кабинет вошли вооружённые люди. - "Я уже распорядился, чтобы вашу семью в целости вывезли с континента. Близ Вильянублы вас ждёт самолёт."

Франко коротко, почти безразлично кивнул. Кано поднялся, а следом за ним вскочили и остальные офицеры: "Счастливого пути, мой каудильо."

Офицеры потянулись к выходу. Кармен мягко положила ладонь ему на плечо. Франко открыл было рот, но не нашёл нужных слов. Он опустил глаза на жену и едва слышно выдохнул:

options.name: "Я всех вас подвёл."

title: Не волнуйся, дорогой
desc:
Ветер трепал волосы Кармен, пока она вглядывалась в горизонт; окружившие её охранники без умолку переговаривались между собой - как всегда, слишком много шума, подумала она. До чего же хотелось сбежать от всего этого - от разброда, от уличных побоищ, от непрекращающейся какофонии гибели, нависшей над ними всеми. Горечь грядущего давила на неё неподъёмным грузом; но тут солдат коснулся её плеча: "Сеньора, самолёт готов. Пора." - Она на мгновение замерла, а затем коротко кивнула.

Кармен обернулась к Франко - тот неподвижно стоял, уставившись в траву под ногами, - и шагнула к мужу, чтобы его утешить: "Пойдём, любимый," - она взяла его за руку, силясь улыбнуться. - "Как только мы покинем страну, всё наладится. Наше добро, наши вещи... мне сказали, они в целости. Карреро уже вылетел, и..."

"А что случится с моей страной?" - голос Франко дрожал от горечи, взгляд всё ещё был прикован к земле. Кармен поглаживала его руку, пытаясь успокоить, но он продолжал. - "Она снова оказалась в смертельной опасности, пока..." - морщины на его лице стали глубже, что заставило Кармен нахмуриться. - "...пока я бегу, как последний трус."

"Ты не трус, дорогой," - мягко возразила Кармен. - "Ты вернёшься. Мы вернёмся. Это наш дом, что бы ни случилось." - Франко наконец поднял глаза, и на его губах мелькнула бледная тень улыбки. - "То, что мы создали, прочнее всего этого. Всё, что ты построил, твоё наследие, всё это переживёт нас."

Франко откашлялся, выпрямился, насколько мог, и посмотрел на самолёт. Помощник подал знак подниматься на борт. Бывший каудильо обернулся к своей жене и безмолвно кивнул. Они устало улыбнулись друг другу и зашагали к трапу. Перед тем как ступить в салон, Кармен замешкалась - где-то вдалеке прогремел взрыв. Но она не решилась обернуться и через миг скрылась в глубине самолёта.

options.name: Испания выстоит. Она должна.

title: Communist Insurgency in Asturias Escalates
desc:
-CONFIDENTIAL-

For the past several weeks, a series of sabotage operations and raids on weapon caches has been reported throughout Asturias (see p. 15-22). While behind-the-lines sabotage operations have been organized by many of the separatist forces, they have usually been pacified within a reasonable timeframe and reduced to isolated cases committed by lone actors or small, isolated cells.

In this case, it has become clear that the Asturias operation was conducted by a large, organized, and cohesive force. Garrison troops were delayed in their response to raids on weapon caches by bridge and railway sabotage, clearly coordinated by the enemy in advance. With much of the military diverted to the frontlines, requests for further assistance had been deferred or outright denied (pp. 23-26).

During the last few days, the situation has clearly reached a critical juncture. Large, disciplined columns have moved into the open, seizing towns and critical roadways and infrastructure. Propaganda leaflets and radio messages by the insurgents have sufficed to ascertain their clear socialistic and communistic ideological leanings. With troops in the region demoralized, outnumbered, and growing increasingly isolated, the commanders of the 17th and 22th Reserve Divisions have made the decision to pull their forces back and to consolidate beyond the borders of the most affected region.

With army forces withdrawn from the region, it appears that the insurgents have already proclaimed a new "workers’ government" and that they are actively preparing to conduct further hostile operations against our forces in order to secure their newfound independence. It is highly recommended that all available troops be diverted to Asturias in order to dismantle their regime before it has the chance to entrench itself.

options.name: We will drive these cockroaches back to their holes.
Arise, you prisoners of want!

title: Meet the New Boss
desc:
Ane pushed her food cart through the chilly Bilbao morning, preparing for the mass of workers to make their way towards the steel factories. The precariously balanced coffee pot and foodstuffs were accompanied by her new transistor radio, bought by Ane’s daughter for her birthday to lighten up her long days at the stall. Arriving at her usual spot, Ane began setting up her coffee pot and stove, humming along with the music.

Suddenly, a wave of static distorted the song, much to Ane’s annoyance. She tried fiddling with it, but the gray-haired vendor had never really understood how the machine worked, and soon gave up. The crackle of static was now all she could hear, until words began to coalesce from the noise.

"...Council of Government. Repeat, this is José María Eskubi, speaker of the Council of Government. This is a special announcement to all citizens of the Basque Country." Ane perked up, but continued setting up her stall.

"The previous government of the Basque Country has failed at defending the freedom of the Basque people from the dangers around us. For this reason, patriots have been forced to take matters into their own hands and ensure that the flame of our freedom is not extinguished. As of today, the Council of Government has been reconstituted according to the principle of maintenance of independence at all costs. All previous government members belonging to the PNV have been relegated from their functions due to their gross negligence in exercising those functions. They have already been replaced by members of the new Council, who are sworn to uphold our principles. This is our duty to you, and to our country. Freedom or death!"

Ane began serving the first workers who had come for her coffee when the music thankfully returned. Governments come and go, but she had more important business to attend to.

options.name: "So, what was this Eskubi guy on about?"

title: The Pain of Brotherhood
desc:
The door burst open without warning. An aide, pale, stumbled to Tarradellas's desk, a stack of reports in her hands. "Mister President, we have an emergency. We have not been able to contact some of our garrisons from the interior, and those we could contact are currently under attack."

"By who?" The President of the Generalitat demanded. He caught one of the reports flying off from his aide's stack. "Is it the Spanish? We shouldn't have trusted them in the first place!"

"No, sir." The aide cut him off. "They're calling themselves the Catalan People's Army. Militias. Workers. Deserters. They're advancing quickly without much opposition."

Tarradellas's eyes widened. It wasn't the Spanish People's Army. It wasn't the Portuguese People's Army. Catalan. It was the same Catalan whom he fought for all these years who threatened to march on Barcelona.

He remembered his 30s so vividly. The hope of a republic. The surge of unity coursing through the veins of the Spanish Republic. But the May Days — that disparaging churning of his stomach when he heard the firing of guns within Barcelona's streets. That tingling in his chest as he looked outside to see brother killing brother. He felt that same churning, that same agonizing tingling in the chest, hearing the Catalan People's Army.

It would not be the Spaniard who brought down Catalonia. It would be the Catalan. The Catalan who could not see eye-to-eye with his fellow countryman. The Catalan who believed in the same rotten ideas of those who had betrayed the Republic in 1937. The Catalan who was willing to shoot, pillage, and kill their people over frivolous ideology.

A united Catalonia, unfortunately, needed some Catalans dead.

options.name: Alza la bandera revolucionaria!
There can be no Catalan unity while the CPA exists.

title: Breaking Point
desc:
Now interrupting your broadcast - an urgent message from Plácido Fernández Viagas, member of the Interprovincial Council of Andalusia.

"I come to address you on the topic of the strife which has ravaged our lands. For months, generals of the Republic have thrown Andalusian men into the meat grinder of the front lines, gaining mere inches for each life lost. Andalusian households have gone hungry as food is diverted to the front, and Andalusian voices have been ignored as the government takes more and more. What have we received in return? Nothing. We have been the backbone of the war efforts for too long, and we will not take any more exploitation.

"As such, the eight provincial deputations have voted with unanimity to no longer support the war effort of the Spanish Republic, and remain neutral in the Iberian wars. Andalusian men will return home, and Andalusian factories will reorient domestically. To all factions on the peninsula, we would like to extend a message of peace - we do not wish for war, and will gladly cooperate with any government who wishes the same. Yet above all else, our priority is to ensure that Andalusia is never mistreated again. Thank you for your attention.

Hundreds of miles away from Sevilla, and just a few miles away from the pounding artillery of the front lines, a squad of soldiers huddled around a radio, listening in shock. One by one, their eyes turned to the youngest soldier in the group - a 19-year-old boy from Murcia, who stood frozen in place. An impossible decision stood before him - the movement he gave his life to on one end, and the world he left behind to join it on the other.

The boy steadied his breath, and made his choice.

options.name: He gave his comrades a weak grin, and switched the radio off.
His rifle fell to his feet, and without a word, he began the long walk back home.

title: Faith Through Strength
desc:
The city held its breath as tanks rolled across the Dom Luís I Bridge.

As soldiers marched in formation down the Avenida da Boavista, the city watched.

As the TVs and radios declared the emergency, Porto realised there was no going back.

Posters were displayed upon walls and trucks drove with speakers upon their rears. The news would be inescapable, there would be no ignorance of the new situation. Portugal itself depending on it, that was the message enforced on every street and checkpoint.

"Porto, the enemies of Portugal persist! The Kingdom lies in continued peril as fear and inadequacy have ruled the hands of those entrusted to return our nation to its peace." The voice of General Kaúlza de Arriaga boomed from every possible place it could, seemingly occupying a stranglehold grip upon broadcasting. On TV screens they watched him, still as a statue behind a podium adorned with the King's colors, denouncing the men he had sworn to defend only yesterday.

"To all across the nation, I give you my earnest promise. Now, myself and men who hold my complete trust guide our destiny. We serve the King, and we shall ensure his realm has its civility restored through any measures necessary. When you see the soldiers upon your streets, take heart. When you hear of my new appointments, give them your faith."

options.name: "If you consider frustrating our efforts through arms or rhetoric, realise your folly and cease."

title: The Southern Break
desc:
Sitting around the meeting table, Humberto Delgado could find no trace of comfort in any of the generals sitting before him. Dour and dark, stained with frustration and effort, none of them met the eyes of his. Absorbed in reports, looking anywhere else, broken hope's miasma hung over the room.

Delgardo read the report titles again, a dozen distributed before him with titles impossible to misunderstand. Attacks on Southern military encampments, many training or medical, by communist forces. "There can be no mistake? This isn't rogue radicals or a misunderstanding or -"

Silence was his answer, a terrible and deep silence. He swallowed, leaning back in his chair. It was some time before one of the generals raised his voice, daring to pierce the haunting quiet.

"Sir, the communists were supportive of our efforts thus far in the war, it may be possible that their opposition may not be universal."

For a moment no one replied, before the officer beside Delgardo crushed the idea. "The Algarve and Alentejo regions are in open revolt. The communists have formed a popular front; that means virtually all of them. Any communist in our territory is an enemy in waiting, while their friends press us from the South and their enemies press us from the North."

One of the generals watched the scene with sympathy, but privately mulled his own options. His sister was in the Algarve, and he had worked with the communists sometimes in the war thus far. He had some good connections - if there was ever a time to leave it was now. Stay true to the Republic, or risk disgrace with the communists? Anchor himself to a potentially sinking ship, or give himself and Portugal a fresh start?

options.name: The Republic will stand so long as good men stand by it; he decided to stay at his post.
The right choices require the most difficult decisions; he decided to abscond south.

title: Newsstands of Spain
desc:
A newsstand in Valladolid. "National Junta overthrown... Yesterday afternoon, officers of the Falange overthrew the Junta, capturing the traitorous Carlos Cano and his ilk... The new government has promised to revive the Falangist revolution, and work closely with our European brothers in Germania..."

A newsstand in Zaragoza. "Kingdom proclaimed in Northwest Spain... After the betrayal of the Junta by the Falangists, Monarchist officers have revolted... José María Valiente Soriano has been chosen as acting regent of the Carlist dynasty until the end of the war... All loyal Spaniards are urged to join the fight for God, Fatherland, and King..."

A newsstand in Sevilla. "Spanish National Junta collapses... After months of infighting, the reactionary government in the north has split in two, between the German-puppeted Spanish National Council and the archaic Kingdom of Spain... Both regimes have declared themselves the one legitimate government of Spain, and fighting has already been reported between the two sides..."

options.name: Yet the Kingdom has promised not to go down without a fight.
The Falangists in the northeast retain much of the strength of the old government...
Yet the Kingdom has promised not to go down without a fight.

title: Report from the Councilor of Defense
desc:
[getdate]
Topic: Alliance with other regional governments

Over the past few months, the political situation in Spain has deteriorated. Actors in the region have become increasingly hostile towards our government, threatening to rob us of our newly gained independence. Outmatched and outgunned, we stand no chance in the case of a Spanish reinvasion.

However, we are not alone in our situation. Separatists and rebels in other regions have successfully broken away from Spain as well, and share the same fear of a potential reinvasion. Due to this, the military high commands of the various breakaway states have been in contact, discussing coordination in the increasingly likely scenario of a war with Spain.

Recently, all parties involved have agreed that the time is ripe to take pre-emptive action against Spain in order to prevent a counterattack and ensure our continued independence. The decision ultimately lies with you, but we advise taking action as soon as possible - Spain will only grow stronger the more we wait.

options.name: United we stand, divided we fall.
iberiawars.29.a

title: Que Non Escampara
desc:
A constant drizzle pattered down on the Spanish troops assembling in Ponferrada. The stone towers of the Templar Castle looming above provided scant protection from the shifting wind and immiserating droplets.

Their sergeant looked over the dripping brows and homesick eyes and spat, "And this is the army that conquered Spain?" The only response was the "plip, plip, plip" of rain on stone.

"No, it damn well isn't!" the sergeant roared, "You bastards thought you were done? Galicia-" a finger jabbed west, "is in the hands of the Portuguese. First they betrayed the Union, and then they grab whatever land and women they like while we're fighting for our lives. You lazy sons-of-bitches would let them take it without drawing a gun? They'd be halfway to Madrid by now if you lot had any say!"

He walked up to a nonplussed soldier, thrusting his hand within a millimeter of the unfortunate man's face, "War's not done until I say it's done, Private Sánchez. Otherwise tugas would be overrunning Badajoz, lugging away your rusted-up motorbike and cow. They'd leave your woman, of course, on account of her being uglier than both."

Before Sánchez could respond, the sergeant was moving on to Private Serrano Ortiz. "I thought, after marching across most of the Peninsula, you'd learn how to tie your damn boots!" A quick glance down confirmed the offending lace, sodden with water, had indeed come undone. "Now I know how an imbecile survived this long, by spending the War face-down in the mud. Get it fucking fixed Serrano - or the only action you'll see is with a Galician cowpat and my tied boot up your ass!"

And so the sergeant paraded on, prodding and assailing, until this miserable little band was praying that the order to march west arrived from HQ. At least it would get them out of here.

options.name: OK

title: Eleven Stars over Andalusia
desc:
It was a good photo; that, Pío Cabanillas couldn't deny.

The clashing of the protestors and police, suspended perfectly in time. The Córdoba streets, supposedly so far from the war, with burnt draft cards and protest signs strewn on the ground. Shattered windows and barricaded shops, signifying the collapse of order in the city. And at the center of the chaos, a young man waving an Andalusian flag, his hair waving in the wind and eyes wild.

He would be more appreciative of the photography skills on display if it hadn't been plastered on the front of every newspaper in Spain.

The riots in Córdoba had sent ripples across the nation, their impact second only to the war itself. Andalusian politicians had grown more and more resistant, threatening to turn off support for the war or even secede entirely. Young activists discussed the resurrection of the Andalusian national identity, with the unnamed boy serving as a symbol of their movement. And in the cities of Spain that had previously been the center of war efforts, dozens of Córdoba bloomed.

Cabanillas threw the boy's photo to the side and put his head in his hands. He had ordered the police to prepare for the protests, but with most resources devoted to the front lines, there was little they could do. The peace had been kept for so long, but Spain was fraying at the seams. If the war didn't end soon, the republic tearing itself apart seemed to not be a matter of if, but when.

options.name: Only when truly angry did the sergeant's Gallego accent creep in.

title: Unthinkable
desc:
TOP SECRET
EYES ONLY
TO AUTHORIZED MEMBERS OF THE REICHSNACHRICHTENDIENST
UNTERNEHMEN BACALHAU

Iberia - Unrecognized - Recently unified under socialist occupation

Following the collapse of organized resistance to the so-called Portuguese People's Republic's invasion of Spain, and the subsequent reunification of Iberia, assessments have been carried out regarding the possibility of regime change.

Sources within the nation have highlighted a weak military, worn down by two large, consecutive campaigns, while trying to professionalize. The economy is virtually nonexistent for the moment, suffering from both the destruction of the Iberian Wars as well as the immediate effects of the mass socialist reorganizations occurring. Politically, they are divided. The populace broadly lacks strong support for the government, apathy being widely reported, while leadership remains torn between competing factions.

Considering these elements, a military solution is recommended to return proper governance to the peninsula. A delay would give Iberia precious time to stabilize, by which time firm measures may be much more costly.

MAY GERMANY BE IN SAFE HANDS.

options.name: The plague of socialism cannot return to Europe.

title: The Gates of South America Reopened
desc:
Report on Colombian Realignment

Context: Colombia's recovery from their civil war, began in 1954 and recently concluded, stalled following the dissolution of their key trade partner, the Iberian Union. Multiple nascent manufacturing operations have declared bankruptcy following the sudden withdrawal of Spanish and Portuguese capital. Additionally, the dominant agricultural sector experienced a sharp downturn as the flow of Iberian shipping, pesticides, and fertilizers ceased.

Economic Impact: In response, Colombia has pursued expanded commercial ties with our market. Shuttered industrial facilities have been temporarily nationalized, with shares then sold to our investors at favorable prices. In return, Colombian economists have hurriedly adapted an existing investment plan from Iberia's economy to our own, and our major importers are gladly purchasing Colombian inventories, especially of coffee, which should help spur a recovery. In all likelihood, these business relationships will become permanent.

Political Impact: Relations with Colombia have markedly warmed, with Bogotá doubling the size of its diplomatic staff pending a physical expansion of their embassy. While no formal changes are expected this year, deeper alignment into our alliance structure is possible. This would be of global significance, given the strategic importance of Colombia's large Atlantic and Pacific-facing ports.

Additional Note: The instability resulting from the end of Iberian commerce and influence in Colombia is likely to be replicated in similarly reliant countries. There is a high probability Colombia is merely the first domino.

options.name: MAY GERMANY BE IN SAFE HANDS
FIDELITY, BRAVERY, INTEGRITY.
ORDEM E PROGRESSO

title: Rerouting the Tankers
desc:
Report on Venezuelan Realignment

Context: Venezuela has seen severe instability since the fall of the Pérez Jiménez military regime in 1958. Naval Commander Wolfgang Larrazábal was unable to consolidate Venezuela's nascent democracy, and his successor was swiftly couped by General Castro León. But ill health plagued the General, and the developmentalist leaders that followed faced significant popular unrest and a communist insurgency. To address these threats, the regime aligned itself with the Iberian Union, which offered markets and limited development and military assistance.

The collapse of the Iberian Union has increased pressure on Venezuela's government and inspired its growing leftist guerilla movement, leading Caracas to seek a new foreign patron. Based on recent diplomatic communiques and commercial exchanges, our country is their preferred choice.

Economic Impact: The primary effect is expected to be heightened access to plentiful, inexpensive Venezuelan oil, though Venezuela's growing internal market will also provide a new source of demand for our manufacturers' consumer goods.

Political Impact: Our replacement of Iberia's role represents another rebuke to the OFN, which lost influence in the country following Castro León's coup. Given the country's strategic position in the Caribbean and territorial claims on Guyana, tensions with the OFN are anticipated to escalate. While Venezuela is not currently seeking to formalize our relationship, any future attempts to do so should be managed carefully to avoid an untimely provocation of the U.S.

Additional Note: Further impacts of Iberia's dissolution are anticipated both in Venezuela and around the globe.

options.name: MAY GERMANY BE IN SAFE HANDS
All roads lead to Rome.
iberiawarspeace.1000.a

title: iberiawarspeace.1.t
desc:
It was the first moment to himself he had all day. After the Republic and its socialists were defeated, Jaime Álvares Pereira de Melo had become the most sought-after man in Portugal. The threat of communism was vanquished, Christian rule was entrenched, and he had become a beacon to all his people. He should have welcomed his newfound status as king. But he could not.

Light shone through the windows of the Sintra National Palace chapel, dragging his shadow every which way across the tiled floor. Outside the chapel doors, dueling advisors jockeyed for his favor, trying to use him as a tool to enact a democratic or authoritarian constitution. Outside the palace gates, German and Italian advisors vied for his support, Portugal and the Monarchy being nothing more than a bit piece in their struggle for Europe. And outside the royal sphere altogether, he knew that thousands of Portuguese saw him not as an emblem of heroism, but as a symbol of the men who killed their husbands, fathers, and sons.

The war may have ended, but only in the presence of God could he be free of strife.

The king looked up towards the cross above the altar. Did he really have the strength to do what must be done? Each movement of his, each little twitch of his arm, was vital to Portugal's future. He may stand at the top of the world, but he had never felt more lost in his life.

Soon, he would have to leave the chapel and fight the wars still raging all around him. Soon, he would be forced to helm the ship and rebuild from the hellish conflict that devastated both the nation and the people. Soon, he would face his trial. But first, he knelt beneath the altar and whispered a prayer, his words forever between him and God alone.

options.name: In the coming years, he would have to savor every moment like this one.

title: iberiawarspeace.2.t
desc:
It had been a day like no other for Humberto Delgado. Parades marching through the streets, planes flying overhead, speech after speech to exuberant crowds, all capped off by a ceremony for him at the São Bento Palace, the parliament of the newly secured Republic. Wine glasses clinked, and politicians of all stripes chatted, giving toasts to the President and all who had made the revolution possible. Slipping out through the back, he made his way across the garden, towards the Prime Minister's residence.

The mansion hadn't had a visitor in months. Dust coated everything - from the furniture, to the empty hearth in the corner, to a jacket on a coat hanger. Delgado slowly walked towards the study and opened the door.

The room was exactly how Salazar had left it. A minimalist and modest desk filled most of the study. Reports, legislation, and correspondence with Franco were sorted into neat stacks. A copy of his autobiography lay on top of a bundle of papers - his unfinished writings. In the near corner, a chessboard with scattered pieces sat next to a list of coordinates and notes, as if trying to recreate and study a position. A ceremonial saber lay on the side of the desk, and a small bookshelf and cabinet were the only other objects in the room. This was all that remained of Portugal's tyrant of nearly thirty years.

Delgado reached for the saber. As if his body was moving on its own, he hacked at the desk with everything he had. Slashes sent wood splinters into the air, and letters and legislation were sliced in two. Half cackling, half shouting, Delgado screamed into the night. "I hope you can hear me in Hell, old bastard! You're fired!" Over and over he swung, until the saber was buried in the wood. Out of breath, he gave one last look towards the sword embedded in the desk, before turning around and leaving Salazar behind for good.

options.name: A new day dawns in Lisbon.

title: iberiawarspeace.3.t
desc:
If one wanted to see the new society of Portugal, one would have to look no further than Commerce Square in Lisbon on the day of victory. All stripes of society mingled and chanted in the square. The pink buildings of the square, once a sign of the bourgeois order that once ruled Portugal, were being spray-painted red. New government officials, many former students no older than their early twenties, milled about with ordinary workers.

Carlos Antunes was happy to be another nameless face in the crowd. From the corner of his eye, he saw an old friend - a steelworker, who had fought under Antunes in the underground against Iberia. The General Secretary hailed him over, fighting and waving to be heard over the bustling square.

The worker looked him up and down. "Well met," he deadpanned, "Mr. Secretary." Antunes broke into a smile, and the two comrades embraced.

They squeezed out of the crowd and walked down to the Tagus River. "Remember the bank robbery in Porto?" "Or the train bombing in Lisbon? I swear, the look on that waiter's face..." The two reminisced about their years of bloody struggle. The friends they made, the comrades they lost, the bodies left in their wake. The wild days of fighting in the streets and sleepless nights hiding from the police. The long, winding road from a cell of under a hundred men, to the vanguards of the revolution in Portugal - and maybe even beyond.

Antunes sat down as they reached the riverbank. "Despite everything... all the pain we've been through... I would do it all again in a heartbeat." He turned to face the worker. "Because now, I can look in the face of any worker, and tell him that he's the equal of the most powerful man in Portugal."

options.name: And the worker didn't just believe Antunes - he already knew.

title: Gilded Vengeance
desc:
Jaime Álvares Pereira de Melo was surrounded, entirely subsumed by the theater around him. Members of the Press, members of the Clergy, the intelligentsia, corporate financiers, and community leaders from all over the country, all converging on the Sala dos Brasões at the Sintra National Palace. All stood in attendance to witness the formal resurrection of the Kingdom of Portugal, the first victim of Antonio Salazar, now risen to deliver last rites to Estado Novo and all who dared receive them.

De Melo felt it improper to consider himself a victim per se, not with so many dead still unburied. Yet for the newly-crowned King of Portugal, the heavy finery wrapped around him only weighed him down like a silk and linen anchorhead, joined by the crown upon his brow for that inevitable, obnoxious idiom of 'heavy is the head that wears the crown.' The royal muttered the speech written for the oh-so-humble Kaúlza de Arriga after the ceremony, partly out of boredom, partly out of contempt.

Kaúlza's speech spelled out the broader itinerary for the GNS, similarly written in the tank columns being readied for the parade after the ceremony. Kaúlza was far from finished; the GNS's war to justify its existence was only just beginning. Portugal itself was just the beginning, and short of marching on Rio de Janeiro, Kaúlza was deadset on reclaiming the glory of Lisbon by any means necessary.

It was then the President of the Council of Ministers, haughty as ever in dress uniform, finally arrived for the ceremony meant for him, the very one Kaúlza himself proposed for himself through backchannels to receive new decorum as 'Savior of the Portuguese Nation.' By this point, King Jaime could only strive to be indifferent, as he was just another cog in a military-political machine that had no purpose or function beyond whatever contrived nonsense Kaúlza was to draw up next.

options.name: Promptly, Kaúlza gave a curt nod to the room, and the ceremony began.

title: Chatter
desc:
From here, they could almost forget the streets below.

Beneath their legs dangling over the crane's ledge, where the breadcrumbs from the tasteless bread they ate fell, the streets of Madrid seemed so distant and otherworldly besides the Almudena Cathedral they were repairing. It appeared as a different world, a vestige spied through a telescope, alien and forbidden to them. Javier and Jorge hungrily chewed, sparing no thought for the long drop before them, and mused upon the cranes in the distance.

"See the Royal Palace? I had to get past that during the fighting; someone blasted holes in it. Why, that tarpaulin covers the whole thing." Javier said, smiling as he relayed the building's affairs. He felt informed, the master of a city that had been harshly reformed.

"Bullshit, you just heard that from someone. Bet you barely came out of your shelter." Javier's face dropped as Jorge rebuffed his information. "Home and this cathedral are probably the most of Madrid you see nowadays. Still, downstairs isn't all bad, got to see those Margaritas earlier. Javier, now there are some women worth fighting for. Woof!"

Javier hit Jorge on his head lightly, earning a soft cry of pain. "Shut up. Like you could fight with your busted leg. They could beat you, or are you going to threateningly waddle in a Republican's direction?"

"I'm rebuilding the King's cathedral, piloting this crane, that'll buy me some points! Maybe I can wear a rosary too. I'll be irresistible."

Both men laughed, sparing not a thought for the approaching end of their break. Beneath them, the ruins of Madrid stretched out, untouched brick shaded brown in the soft afternoon sun.

options.name: The King will return to his rightful home and a coronation; the masses shall take refuge in that.

title: Mirror, Mirror
desc:
The Palace of El Pardo, on the north end of Madrid, looked more like a condemned building than a warzone. Parts of the building had been entirely burnt out, and where it wasn't was utterly ransacked. Shattered glass everywhere, upturned furniture with trash and debris strewn all over the place. Here or there, a mosaic of bullet holes in the wall, spent shell casings across the floor. Carlos Iniesta Cano spied a spent shell casing as it rolled over and bounced harmlessly off the side of his boot.

The President of the newly reformed Junta looked upon the carnage with muted disbelief. Past the bullet holes and broken glass, Cano spied the velvet carpet and silk curtains, the slashed paintings and overturned liquor cart, peering into the world Francisco Franco actually lived in. This was the realm the great generalissimo had carved for himself? This was what so many of Cano's peers had religiously given their lives and their careers to protect? A coterie of backroom aristos in khaki, gorging themselves on wine and hors d'oeuvres?

Generations of service in the Exército, not just his, but many other comrades. Many of them killed in action, many of them decades ago, all flashed through Cano's mind. Dejected, Cano moved to the overturned cart, reaching down and pulling a bottle from underneath it; Chilean Red, 1899, a decent year. Bottle in hand, he spied graffiti on a distant wall in the hallway just past the doorway, surrounded with Republican slogans in bloody red, likely from sympathetic youth who couldn't take a hint.

Cano almost chuckled at the thought, picturing his Carlist allies just crestfallen and incensed. He realized there was no real revelation to be had here, just the confirmation of what had already, obviously, been the case after all. As he cracked the bottle and began downing small, measured gulps, he dreamt of the future Franco often spoke of, but never delivered. The future he and the Junta dreamt of delivering, the one for which no one else now stood to stop them.

options.name: Spain would be pure, refined, and distilled.

title: Valle de los Caídos
desc:
They had parted for her when she came to Valle de los Caídos, but none knew of what she had spoken of. Only who she spoke to.

As she'd walked past the haggard prisoners digging, some of them had recognized her. They stayed silent, heads bowed as they toiled in the huge holes they tore into the earth. The pilgrims to the site moved aside, whispers passing through the crowds both ahead and behind her. When she reached the threshold of the tomb, she found it encircled but deserted within.

Pilar Primo de Rivera had come to visit her brother.

They had watched as she had entered, unsteady steps and heavy breaths betraying her impassive face. Eyes holding a flood none dared to comment upon, all denied seeing. They all came to see the martyr, the man whose vision would now save Spain, but this moment was not for them. They stood in the baking sun, maintaining a vigil upon the stone tomb. Battered, but standing nonetheless. They would take from its example.

After some minutes, Rivera emerged. On the tomb's threshold, she stood stoically, but the clues of events within could be seen by those who looked. Her eyes were reddened, hints of moisture just about visible upon her cheeks. Her voice was raw, almost wavering between strength and sadness, but holding itself steady enough to trick the unobservant few.

What words had she spoken to her brother? What confessions or regrets? Promises or pleas? It mattered little as she spoke to the surrounding pilgrims, and to all Spain. They all made their own answer, their own vision of history. Old Spain had entered, and within the voice ringing around them, they heard something new.

"¡Caídos por Dios y por España!"

options.name: The answer came, the crowd adopting a single voice. "José Antonio—¡Presente!"

title: The Lighthouse Upon the Rocks
desc:
The long room, teeming with hastily assembled attendees, fought over the limited floor space. The black and white tiles, immaculate and shiny, were invincible under the army of feet upon them. People jostled. The Palacio de San Telmo had not seen such numbers descend on it in living memory; the news of the meeting had spread far beyond the intended ears. Pio Cabanillas' 'debate club', Political Action, had gathered amongst a sea of intruders.

Pio stood at the end of the room, balanced on a stool. The news of the victory, the official surrender, had left no time to properly arrange this meeting. But even as the room before him brimmed past the point of occupancy, he felt unable to demand exclusivity. Today was a day for all, and he would share it with them.

Over the deafening crowd, he began. "Thank you, to all here today. Even to our unexpected guests, I bid you welcome too. I am glad to have you here, for I intend to forward today a proposal for all Spain, regardless of which side they fought for." Some murmurs of approval, but most listened, hanging upon his words.

"I was informed last night that the final surrender had been signed. Spain is once again free." Cheers from the PA members, as well as some of the public. "But we cannot think that this is victory. Freedom has come before to Spain, and it was lost each time. King and Caudillo have afflicted this land, this nation now reduced to ruin. We cheer, but I ask you how many have died so that we can cheer?" Silence.

"Today should be a day of celebration, but we must realize the task before us. Spain needs a real debate upon what this Republic means and the values for which it will stand. We must accept responsibility for the sacrifices made for the better day we now enter. We must wash away the horror of the war, and with an election, trust our voices will make something better."

options.name: Pio saw the face of Manuel Fraga in the crowd. He applauded, and the applause spread like wildfire.

title: Oracle
desc:
Sitting in the small, desolate room he had been quartered in, looking at the grainy footage of Madrid on the tiny TV, Jamie dos Santos Serra almost began to regret his post. Instead of enjoying the festivities of Lisbon, Madrid, or any of the numerous cities no doubt celebrating the impending restoration of the Union, he was here. Sitting almost naked on a bed in a room that smelt of rot and mold, teetering on the edge of a cliff in the Pyrenees.

He had envisaged the Minister of Defense role to have been a bit more glamorous.

It had rained all day as he'd walked in and out of bunkers, entrenched positions, and observation posts. The geography was as familiar to him now as the contours of his own body, each valley and road thoroughly photographed and enlarged. He'd listened and nodded as maps had been brought to him, notations of French movements barely more than a few dozen kilometers away.

He shook his head and lay on the bed, trying to find some comfort in the thin mattress as he stared at the cracking paint of the ceiling. The compressed voices of Antunes and Carrillo, almost unrecognizable thanks to the poor television speaker and reception, proclaimed plans to unify Portugal and Spain once more. How grand it must be to chant in the streets of festive, liberated cities.

He ignored the footage - it seemed hollow. They celebrated like victory had come, but every day, more guns appeared across the border. International volunteers they couldn't disrupt, aerial reconnaissance they couldn't combat, material they just couldn't match. Everywhere he had seen his brothers, Portuguese and Spanish, hardened by the decades of guerrilla campaigns, amongst green troops whose hands shook. All learning the new reality of their war, unable to hide and using the salvaged remnants of the Union military. The true reckoning was yet to come; the hordes of European reaction were at the door.

options.name: He closed his eyes to sleep, the TV continuing unheard. A restless sleep, plagued by visions.

title: Washed Away Upon History's Current
desc:
I bobbed up and down, the cold water of the Tagus controlling me completely. I was one with the river, slave to its whims, cast from my perch above. I was never to return. The bridge above us is now alien in every sense.

The streets above had burst with life as I had watched, some of those shouting even climbing upon myself to get a better view. The loud, endless chants of foreign diesel engines moved past as the people tried to climb atop them. Laughing, singing, crying, and cheering all reverberated around those metal boxes moving upon the road, the men atop them fresh-faced and grinning in the midday light. They looked different from the men I had seen leave before. They had marched, stone-faced, out of the city, and then later other men had come in their place. Hadn't there been celebration then? Hadn't there been destruction? I couldn't understand, the faces were never the same and only ever grew older.

The loud vehicles and marching men soon passed, replaced with a single convoy of open-top vehicles. Banners proclaiming these men hung above them as the spectators standing with me cried out titles for them. The old guard, the true patriots, the nation's greatest: all honors I heard thrust upon these men with long faces and worn skin. They smiled, but their eyes were weary and their waving weak.

But for me, the festival was over. Someone saw me and climbed from his vehicle, pouncing at me. When the people saw me, and who was coming for me, they cheered. There was no support in them, their apathy lost in a moment. They saw me, a bystander, and cheered as I was torn from my place and held aloft.

"I, Colonel João Varela Gomes, declare this bridge liberated!" he cried to roars of approval as I was cast below, the symphony of emotion and material fading as the Tagus took me. I shared the river with many others, and together our fate was tied to the current.

options.name: Water lapped over the sign as it was carried away from History. Upon it was printed: Salazar Bridge.

title: Matadouro
desc:
Pain. A searing, awful pain that never seemed to let up. It ached deeply, piercing into his bones, threatening to split open his skin and reveal the bruised muscle and stretched sinew within his battered legs. And yet, he was nonetheless dragged from the crowd to his allotted spot upon the limestone wall, where men and women wept and glowered and cradled their arms in fright. When they finally let go of him, he slumped down against the stone. It hardly mattered if he stood. He drew a shaky hand against the wall, feeling the familiar pockmarks where bullets had once struck.

Communists, Atlantic capitalists, freemasons, and their government lackies. They would all soon receive their place against the walls of the Tower. Her towering visage loomed over the armed Blueshirts and their prisoners; if Belém had a face, all of Lisbon would surely see her weep. With little fanfare, the guards let slip the safeties of their rifles, taking aim at their prisoners. None of their cries escaped the torrent of gunfire that followed, a cruel silence settling across the square.

"More," the Captain murmured, gesturing for an aide to draw closer. Upon the aide's lapel, a small, golden badge shimmered with the insignia of the PIDE. "Not enough in the crowds. Bring a bigger batch tomorrow." Drawing his gaze over the terrified onlookers nearby, the Captain's expression soured. "Empty the regional jails if you have to. Make a statement."

"At once, sir." The aide grinned as nearby Blueshirts dragged the freshly executed away in trails of blood. "The disobedience of Lisbon will soon be but a distant memory. With this display, the Falange is ascendant over all of Portugal!" Such honeyed words from the aide were met only with silence from the Captain, his steely gaze still fixed upon the crowd. With every taut noose and public fusillade, the march towards purity seemed further out of reach than ever. And yet, the slaughter would continue, for they knew little else. Slaughter for the sake of slaughter. A self-fulfilling prophecy.

title: The Charm
desc:
The wind rustled through the leaves of Casa de Campo, sending small waves through the placid lake, painted gold by the setting sun. General Delgado was walking on the lakeside promenade alongside Chief of Staff José Miguel Vega Rodríguez, letting the precious moments of quiet wash over him. De Sena and the other suits could hash out all the necessary details of peace with their counterparts in the restored republic. He wanted to come here with a man who could understand war.

The two men turned from the lake, walking for a while under an archway of darkening gold and purple before Delgado suddenly broke the silence, looking his companion straight in the eye. "Señor Vega. A Spanish Republic has already fallen twice this century. One of those times, you even contributed to its downfall. Do you think this third republic will be able to keep itself together?"

Vega was taken aback for a moment, but quickly regained his composure. He let the question settle before pointing to the bullet-ridden fountain behind Delgado. "You know, Senhor Delgado... back during the first Civil War, I fought against the Republic's soldiers. They'd fought and died for their dream in this park, in this city, all around Spain. Thirty-something years later, I was the commander of the Republic's soldiers, and again, they'd been willing to die for something much greater than me or my orders. Both times, the Republic fought with its back to the sea, surrounded by enemies much stronger than it, and both times it fought with tenacity and true valor."

Vega took a deep breath and shook Delgado’s hand. "I know the Republic's soldiers will fight just as well now."

options.name: And it would never be enough.

title: The Unimaginable Triumph
desc:
The soldiers of the Portuguese Exército were lined up along the boulevard, but they did not hide the faces of the hundreds of Spaniards behind them. On their faces was the same absence of words King Jaime Álvarez Pereira de Melo had been stricken with since the news of the Spanish surrender. The Iberia beyond the bullet-proofed windows of the royal limousine seemed more like a painted dream at times, but the looks of humiliation, confusion, and disbelief on everyone that floated by spoke to the harsh reality that the war had brought.

It was supposed to be impossible, relegated to the stuff of ahistorical wet-dreams from armchair nationalists with delusional pipe dreams of Portugal dominating its Hispanic neighbor. Yet the reincarnated Kingdom of Portugal had miraculously emerged victorious, the institutional grandfather to the Iberian Union had routed not only the Salazarists that had killed it, but their Francoist imitators in Madrid and all others who sought the levers of power for themselves.

The motorcade slowed to a stop outside the Almudena Cathedral. Inside, the leadership of the Carlist regime installed by Kaúlza waited alongside representatives of the House of Bourbon, soon to be crowned as the Kings and Queens of Spain for the first time in generations. Even if much of the pageantry was to fluff Kaúlza's ego, everyone else was just content with a defined conclusion of Iberia's collapse and the return of long-term peace.

As the rear door opened, the sun beamed brightly, almost too much so. Light shone down upon the ancient medieval frescos of one of Europe's most storied cities. Even with visible scars all across the city from the heavy fighting, Madrid's beauty remained, imperious and invincible. The King felt the artist in him come alive, his heart lightened and swelled. What happened to Iberia was a tragedy, but the beauty spoke of a true ever after: A new and beautiful future for both countries, clothed in the traditions of the old.

options.name: Like an old love affair, the crown heads of Spain and Portugal, united once again!

title: Born in the Azure
desc:
Far above his head, the portcullis towered over Kaúlza de Arriga, dwarfing him.

Somewhere behind him, he heard the scribbling of a fountain pen. "It is done."

Kaúlza offered no reply, still captivated by the castle façade: Olivenza, a small town, with an inconsequential population of a few thousand. This place had been Portuguese once, ruled by the monarchy before it was seized by Napoleon and ceded to his Habsburg puppets in Madrid. At the time, it was seen as the nail in the coffin for Portugal's ability to militarily outfight the Spaniards; now Kaúlza stood before this monument to an older era, internalizing that his determination had accomplished something that had been a foregone impossibility.

"It...i-it is done." The same voice, more demure, repeated behind him. Kaúlza was still lost in history as he turned to face him. The Generalissimo took the papers in hand. "Your security is assured." He said, eying the documents detailing Spain's new military regulations, as well as surrendering military equipment to the Exército. "Armies are quite expensive. It is better this way."

The poor man forced a brave smile, saying little. The PIDE agents in Madrid would make sure no one in the new regime got any ideas, but this one should have a fruitful career, so long as he played nice. "Inform your colleagues that Olivenza is under my administration, effective immediately and indefinitely." Kaúlza felt merciful, offering a stiff pat on the minister's shoulder as he left to see inside the castle for the day.

options.name: "Even in Olivenza, the road still leads to Rome..."

title: Remembering Names
desc:
He had seen thousands of trees. Millions maybe. But this one. This one was beautiful. The jacaranda blossoms floated downwards, traversing through the infinitude of pathways, swinging left and right, until they landed on the stone tombs. And they lay there. And then another would land.

 José Miguel Vega Rodríguez had been in war. He had been in Russia. He had been in Morocco. But he had never been to Prazeres Cemetery.

"Alejandro Luz."

The general looked up. The pastor called another name. Then another. But Alejandro. His eyes fluttered. His right cheek gave a couple of twitches. Vega closed his eyes, trying to remember where he had heard of Alejandro Luz before.

Right. Ifni. They were stationed there for a couple of years. Vega tried to remember what Alejandro was like. They had maybe two conversations. Nothing memorable. Vega tried to frown, but nothing moved. He looked to his right at Delgado.

"Alejandro Luz. I think I knew him. Good kid," Vega whispered to Delgado. Delgado nodded without turning his head. "But, this service, Delgado... This has been going on for hours by now. Iberia... the lives..."

"Those who lie here would be proud that Iberia is finally at peace," Delgado whispered back, eyes still on the pastor. "Our Republic, General, cannot let these lives go to waste."

Vega nodded. That tree had disappeared. Another of the millions of trees he had seen before. He looked at the pastor.

"Danilo Noceda. Emanuel Cunha. Caio Henriques..."

options.name: There is no greater guilt in realizing you can no longer cry.

title: Severance
desc:
"Señores." General Iniesta Cano was standing on the wide steps of the neoclassical São Bento Palace, the former seat of the Portuguese parliament and cooperative chamber. He was flanked by ten Spanish Legionnaires, filling the space between him and the sculpted statues on both sides of the staircase and glowering at the audience.

Cano had served the Iberian military for long enough to speak passable Portuguese, but he was not here as a friendly Iberian officer, but as a conquering Spanish general. They will understand his Spanish, or live in ignorance. "I hereby proclaim that, following the recent armistice, the territory of Portugal shall be occupied by Spain for as long as necessary for a proper governing structure to be established, one that will maintain the cherished traditions of the Portuguese people and cordial relations with the Spanish state. The costs of the occupation will be indemnified to Spain in full by this government once it is established, in order to help in Spain's own post-war reconstruction."

Cano put down his papers, surveying the crowd that had come to hear his pronouncement -  Portuguese officers, statespeople, and civilians. Some looked at him with trepidation, others dejectedly kept their eyes on the ground, watched by his legionnaires. Yes, Portuguese officers - not Spanish, and certainly not Iberian. It was time to put that lie, which has tied Spain down for so long, in its place.

He cleared his throat, looking straight at the camera. "However, this occupation is and will never be a step towards a new Union. Spain is Spain, and Portugal is Portugal, and the folly of any attempts to hide this truth has been laid bare across the fields and trenches of this land and ours. Once Portugal's new government is able to stand on its own two feet, I will be the first to congratulate it for its independence."

options.name: They will applaud him, one day.

title: Song of the Marching Requetés
desc:
The streets of Porto echoed long into the night, as wine-flushed Spaniards marched through the now-occupied city. Heedless of the men they killed and people beneath their boots, one voice starts, and the rest follow:

"When Javier comes king again,
Hurra! Hurra!
We'll give him a throne to sit on then,
Hurra! Hurra!
And Spain will cheer, with Lisbon's shouts
The traitors, they will all be rout
And we'll all feel gay when Javier comes king again!

"When Franco sought to cut us out,
Hurra! Hurra!
When all of Europe cast their doubts,
Hurra! Hurra!
We never flagged, we never failed,
We fought until we had prevailed,
So we'll all feel gay when Javier comes king again!

"Get ready for the Requetés,
Hurra! Hurra!
We're coming home in red berets,
Hurra! Hurra!
With medals pinned, and victories won,
And stories for the youth beyond,
For we'll all feel gay when Javier comes king again!"

options.name: For we'll all feel gay when Javier comes king again!
iberiawarspeace.21.a
iberiawarspeace.22.a

title: An Uneasy Partition
desc:
Valencia is liberated, and is now under control of the state. Mostly.

Territorial control is not absolute, being split between ourselves and the Catalonians - a state of affairs that can be described as uneasy at best. It is clear to all that this reality cannot endure, and that some decisive resolution will be required.

As both of us are members of the AFCP it is unlikely (but pointedly not impossible) that physically violent escalation will occur, especially as a split occupation will intensify demands for a referendum. The Catalonians have been pushing for just that, and it is likely that their agitators will continue their efforts with ever stronger commitment, as will ours.

We must control this process. If we can establish strong rules of shared occupation, expand our control of the region (especially if we can secure all of it), and otherwise work to de-escalate tensions, we can improve our position in the event of any future referendum. It will be an intensive process - but the potential prize cannot be denied.

options.name: Start dialing.

title: A Proposed Summit
desc:
An official communication has been sent to us by the Republic regarding the split occupation of Valencia. They wish to negotiate, and politically we must be receptive to this.

While there are those in the government who think its a mistake to engage in dialogue at all, most realize the opportunity present in any negotiations, especially given the tension present in the divided region. If our representatives play their cards right, and we are very careful in what we say, promise, do and imply, we can not only preserve the split but work to expand our territory within it.

Were that to happen, in the future it could be we who could call for a referendum;in such a situation the outcome could only be beneficial to our interests. As such, it has been decided. We will respond positively and should the Republic continue their course after reading our initial position we will sit down formally with them.

We must not miss the opportunity presented.

To the table we go.

options.name: Lets hope this pays off

title: Setting the Terms
desc:
Catalonia has responded positively to our message and although secrecy must be maintained owing to the ongoing conflicts, talks can commence.

It is essential that beyond holding the talks in an undisclosed location, that the press remains unaware, that guests (if any) be restricted only to the most necessary, and that security be carefully controlled. In any such negotiation, information will be king and we must ensure that we are the ones who control it.

Before any of that, however, we must provide instructions to our representatives. There are only two real positions at the moment that are broadly acceptable - either we propose keeping the current split occupation (and hope to progress our control later on), or we push for full control now.

Both options have potential upsides and downsides - but one must be chosen. Which should it be?

options.name: We are willing to keep the split occupation.
We demand that Catalonia withdraws.

title: The Continued Divide
desc:
The Republic's position has been made clear - they wish to maintain the current split occupation.

It is likely that they, similar to ourselves, can ill-afford any additional conflict at the moment, and wish to be able to dedicate their attention elsewhere. This is understandable, and we can of course accept this reinforcement of the status quo without addition. It would certainly assist us in doing the same.

Or, as has been proposed by some, we can work to achieve more, leveraging the Republic's desire to move on, and attempt to append some additional small victories to the agreement. Several figures in our government have been pushing for a reduction in commercial restrictions, and in convincing the Republic to allow Catalonian business in their occupation zones.

This could be a boon for us if accepted - or it could lead to a demand for reciprocity. What shall be our response?

options.name: Accept the deal as is.
We want Catalonian businesses to operate on both sides.

title: An Economic Concession?
desc:
The Catalonian response has been received - and it is positive, though it does come with a 'request' for concessions.

Fundamentally, they indicate that the split occupation is acceptable, but in exchange they wish for Catalan businesses to operate freely across all of Valencia. This was not a wholly unexpected request, as economic presence within the state would be extremely helpful to their nascent economy, but it must be carefully considered.

Voices have emerged advocating for the Catalonian demand since, they claim, allowing such activity would not likely constitute a significant threat and demonstrate benevolence on our part. Others highlight that while perhaps insignificant in the near term, we must express caution for the long term due to the foothold this would give their Republic in our zone, and as such we should reject the condition. A third group suggests accepting the request in order to maintain the split occupation while also requesting the same treatment for Republic business within the Catalonian zones. It is only fair, after all.

What should the Republic's official response be?

options.name: No. Catalan businesses will be treated as foreign enterprises.
We can allow this - if the same treatment is given to our businesses.
Yes. We will allow free access to Catalonian businesses.

title: Pushing the (Military) Envelope?
desc:
Success - for now, at least.

The Republic has capitulated on the matter of economic activity within Valencia in return for our cooperation in maintaining the split occupation. Catalonian businesses will have free access to conduct affairs across the region, and this will help our nation and people tremendously. They now ask to finalize the talks. We could do that.

We could also, as some in our delegation have suggested, continue to push further. Capitulating on this issue shows weakness on the Republic's part and it is possible that we may be able to extract more concessions. In particular, our military officers have asked that we push for military jurisdiction across both occupation zones, in order to better capture saboteurs and spies.

The Republic would never accept this without reciprocity for their own forces, but that would be acceptable. The question is, do we attempt to get their 'agreement' on this?

options.name: Ask the Republic for the militaries to each have jurisdiction across zones.
We've gotten enough. Don't risk it, sign the deal.

title: Further Pressure
desc:
Our concession on Catalonian economic activity seems to have had the opposite result to what was intended. They are pushing further, and we must decide how to reply.

It is clear that their military has had a say in their latest communication - they wish for their forces to have cross-border jurisdiction across both Valencian occupation zones, ostensibly to better pursue and capture saboteurs, spies, and other agitators. They are smart enough to know we would never accept this unilaterally, and so offer the same rights to our forces in exchange. This 'offer', such as it is, has provoked intense discussion in our delegation.

Some demand we reject it outright as a blatant attempt at pushing the interests of their Republic by the backdoor, others see value in a reduced version limited to police forces which would better allow us to contain their presence, and still others suggest we accept it in order to exploit and turn their gambit onto them - hopefully in better fashion than the Catalonians will do to us. What shall our choice be?

options.name: Absolutely not. Reject this.
Suggest downgrading the cross jurisdiction to police forces.
Accept this. We have ideas on how to exploit it.

title: A Firm Rejection
desc:
Our request for cross-zone military jurisdiction, even with reciprocation, has been flatly rejected by the Republic.

In no way, they say, will they allow Catalonian military forces into their occupation zone. The split of Valencia, the response read, will be firm and carefully controlled, with each force strictly constrained within the zone assigned.

They further insist that their concessions on economic activity were generous as it is, and have made it very clear that no further negotiations will be acceptable or entertained. We must choose to either accept the current understanding and sign the agreement, or reject it and walk away.

What instructions should we send to our delegates?

options.name: We've gotten enough. Sign it.
Not good enough. Do not sign it.

title: A Final Proposition?
desc:
The Spanish response to our offer of joint jurisdiction over both parts of the occupation has been positive. We now have guaranteed business access to all parts of the liberated zones, and the military access to back that access up in case the Spaniards try any underhanded meddling. For many in the Catalan delegation, this is a triumph in and of itself - our forces will stand on equal footing with those of the Spanish and force them to hold to their own end of the deal, and also build legitimacy with the people.

However, some in the delegation have proposed trying to push our advantage further with a final proposal to the Spanish. They envision the establishment of a civilian council, composed of members of both sides, to oversee and manage the occupation as well as handle any breaches of the agreement. As the militarily weaker side, this will mostly benefit us - otherwise, the Spanish may still attempt to force any issue in a manner favorable to them. This council will, at least in theory, be able to tie the hands of any rogue actors on the ground and guarantee at least some stability in both zones.

The proponents of this idea claim it will provide a solid guarantee for a stable occupation and that the Spanish would not have to give up very much - they have already agreed to a shared jurisdiction, this would just be a way to officialise it further and tackle any breaches of the agreement. It would also formalize our own influence in their zone, an invaluable commodity.

On the other hand, many of the Delegation's members believe that the current agreement in place is a good enough guarantee - the Republic wouldn't want to embroil itself in another conflict while the War raged. Furthermore, trying to push through this perk has potential to backfire, with the Spanish seeing it as an unnecessary humiliation, rather than a potential benefit, which could threaten everything we have achieved so far.

options.name: Sign the agreement as is.
We want an overseeing civilian council.

title: An Overseeing Civilian Council?
desc:
After agreeing to the Catalonian proposal for a joint military jurisdiction of the recently liberated territories, most members of our delegation believed that this was the end of it - surely, the Catalans would not be able to muster any more objections and demands. The road to a final agreement was wide open - or so we thought.

The Catalan delegation, apparently willing to go to any lengths to extract even the smallest concession, has come up with an additional request: not only do they want joint armed jurisdiction over the territory, they're now asking for the establishment of a civilian council to oversee the overall occupation, to be composed of officials from our side and theirs. This council is supposed to legally enforce the agreement, address any complaints and punish rogue actors on the ground.

On the face of it, there isn't much to oppose in this proposal - its only real purpose is the enforcement of terms we've already agreed to and would have a hard time undermining, at least while the War lasts. While disproportionately benefitting the Catalans, as the militarily weaker side of the agreement, we could use it as a forum for our own complaints and ensure they hold their own side of the deal.

However, some in our delegation are outraged. They claim that, having approached the Catalans with an offer of friendship, this attempt to bind our hands shows that they lack the minimal level of trust required for a true alliance to take shape. They say this council will hamstring any efforts to restore order in the region and make us look weak in the defense of the national interest, diplomatically and even militarily. What the people in these territories need, they argue, is effective government and relief, not Catalonian separatists playing political games with our ability to provide for them.

options.name: It's not much more of a concession than what we've already made...
We've been more than generous until now, but we're not pushovers.

title: The Spanish Reject the Civilian Council!
desc:
Following a few days of deliberation, the Spanish delegation has replied to us, rejecting the idea of a civilian overseeing council.

They claim that the very request shows a "lack of trust and of responsible statesmanship" on our side. In their view, our shared struggle calls for solidarity and compromise, not attempts to stay on top of one another. Additionally, they say, even if they had wanted to undermine the joint occupation (which they promise has never been their intention), the joint armed occupation would make such an endeavor too costly - those resources would be better spent fighting the War, just as the resources the civilian council would require would be.
