Many in our delegation, while not pleased, can understand the Spanish viewpoint. After all, we had already been prepared to sign an agreement before deciding to add this proposal. It would be helpful to have but, as some in the military say, our forces can handle any potential rogue actors themselves and the resources could be spent elsewhere.

However, some of the more hawkish delegates claim that this rejection shows the Spanish never intended to keep up their end of the bargain. They claim that without the oversight council, the Republic will use its superior military force to undermine the shared occupation and attempt to present us with a fait accompli in the region when the War concludes. While the Spanish claim that our request shows a lack of trust, these delegates say that this rejection shows the Spanish could not have been trusted to begin with.

options.name: Forget about the oversight council, we'll handle this through the armed forces.
No council, no deal.

title: A Shared Police Jurisdiction?
desc:
The Spanish delegation has come back to us, after taking a couple of days to consider our request for joint military jurisdiction over the occupied region. While the delegates claim that their government is not inherently opposed to the idea of joint jurisdiction, they have mentioned various concerns with the idea of joint military control, particularly the allocation of resources better spent elsewhere in the war effort and the difficulty of coordinating both forces. Instead, they suggest that the joint jurisdiction will be shared between both of our police forces.

Some in our delegation see this proposal as reasonable enough. We could also benefit by redirecting our forces elsewhere and, with help from the Spanish, our police forces should be able to handle any issues arising from the occupation. Our police forces still have similar structures and are less sensitive to sharing information, so coordinating them would be far easier than trying to coordinate our militaries. They also point out that having the police maintain order instead of the military will help return the region to normalcy sooner, better setting the grounds for a postwar referendum.

However, other members of our delegation view this counteroffer with skepticism. They claim that the downgrading of the joint occupation force will allow the Spanish to come in and assert themselves at any point, using their superior military force, with no equivalent force on our side to prevent them from doing so. They also claim that the Spanish will have an easier time manufacturing crises if the area is under less direct military control. A few have even taken the step of claiming that the Spanish offer is an attempt to set up an incident which will allow them to sweep in and take the whole of the region for themselves.

options.name: This extra manpower would be useful on the front line. Accept the compromise.
We may yet have to fight this Spanish government too. Reject, and be ready.

title: The Catalans Reject Joint Police Jurisdiction
desc:
When our delegates suggested downgrading the shared jurisdiction of the newly occupied territories to the police level, many of the Catalan delegates were visibly displeased. However, it was hoped that their government would see reason and cut down on the resources necessary to administer the region - resources which would be better spent on the war effort instead of political games. However, this appears not to have been the case. The Catalans have responded in the negative, saying that they will only accept a mutually-agreed, joint military occupation of the territory. Now, they have passed the onus of decision back to our side.

On the face of it, we could be flexible - we have more military resources than the Catalans, and while we would prefer using them elsewhere, this disparity could be leveraged to our advantage in any future negotiations over the region. Showing magnanimity to the small breakaway region in this way will also all but guarantee that they sign the agreement.

However, some of our delegation's members see this as a naked attempt to weaken us in the face of a common enemy, in order to further the sectarian interests of the breakaway governments. These delegates claim that tying down our forces in the rear will put an outsized burden on our frontline military operations, forcing us to rely more heavily on the Galeusca governments. This agreement was supposed to safeguard Spain but now, they say, it may as well guarantee its dismemberment if signed as is.

options.name: We'll be generous, but make it clear that we will not budge any further.
We will not be held hostage by separatists!

title: The Spanish Accept Joint Military Jurisdiction
desc:
Many members of our delegation have been anxious after we have expressed our dissatisfaction at the idea of downgrading the unified jurisdiction of the occupied territories to merely a joint policing force. The Spanish could very well have considered that as an attempt to divert their forces from the frontlines and give us and the other Galeusca members further edge in future negotiations.

Now, however, our delegates can breathe a sigh of relief. The Spanish have relented, whether out of genuine goodwill or as an attempt to show magnanimity. Both of our militaries are to have jurisdiction over the area, as originally planned. The more hawkish members of our delegation see this success as a vindication of their efforts to drive as hard a bargain as possible with the Spanish, perhaps attempting to set the tone of future diplomatic relations. Yet, there are limits to what hawkishness can get us, especially with the war still ongoing and our limited power compared to the Spanish. Their delegation has let us know in no uncertain terms that, while they were willing to be magnanimous, they will not be making any further concessions to us and any attempt by us to push for more will result in the immediate termination of the negotiations.

With our goals mostly achieved, most of our delegates view this as fair. Most outstanding issues can be left for later - now is the time to sign this agreement and relish our diplomatic success, and the further legitimacy it will grant us on the world stage.

options.name: A toast to our foreign office!

title: The counterproposal
desc:
Instead of accepting our deal outright, the Republic has presented an interesting counterproposal. They are willing to accept the presence and operation of our businesses inside their zone, on condition that we allow their businesses to operate in ours. While this deal will surely benefit both our economies as well as provide more goods to the populace, taking some relief efforts away from the occupational authorities that can be redirected elsewhere.

However, some remain skeptical. The fear of the Valencian economy becoming dominated by Spanish companies, even in our zone, is present within the delegation and could be a source of future Spanish agitation. Their economic power dwarfs our own and we may risk effectively losing influence in our own zone. Furthermore, some even argue that, given the right diplomatic maneuvering, we could instead get the Republic to agree to our original proposal. We must tread carefully as allies are valuable at the moment, it may be unwise to test our relations with the Republic by pushing them too far. It is equally unwise, however, to compromise our position in the region to potential imperialists.

options.name: The deal sounds fair, let's accept it.
Our proposal was firm but fair;, it's that or nothing.

title: The Catalonian reply
desc:
TheCatalonians have rejected our offer, stating that while they respect the spirit of reciprocity, Catalan businesses must be protected due to their weaker economy. This has gone down like a lead balloon among many in our delegation, cursing that even a simple request for some reciprocity was too much for separatists. Their posture makes it difficult to hold any further negotiations as capitulation on this would appear a surrender to the Catalan government against our own interests. Numerous delegates are suggesting that this is where the negotiations should end.

But as much as we want to punish their selfishness, this might be the worst time to do it. Some members of the delegation continue to argue for acceptance of the deal and continuation of the negotiations. They argue that the Catalonians do have a point regarding our uneven economies, and that the very last thing we can use in a time like this is more enemies. But is that worth compromising one of our regions to the separatists?

options.name: Fine, accept the deal.
Catalan arrogance ends here, and so do the negotiations.

title: A masterclass in diplomacy
desc:
Success! The Republic has accepted our original deal. This means that we can reap all the benefits, while still having guaranteed economic dominance over our part of Valencia. This is a major victory for the Catalan economy.

However, everything comes at a cost. While the Republic accepted our deal, they are not in the best mood after we rejected their counterproposal. We will have to be very careful with our actions in the coming months if we want to maintain any form of diplomatic relations with them. So the best course of action at this moment is to sign the deal, thank them for their cooperation and quietly leave. We have gotten what we bargained for.

options.name: Another Catalan victory!

title: A disappointing answer
desc:
The Republic has denied our proposal of letting our businesses operate in all of Valencia. Our following actions have to be carefully considered if we want to keep the negotiations alive. Our strategy of trying to staple other deals to the agreement has already failed. This leaves us with three main options.

The first option is to play it safe. The Republic has clearly shown it is only interested in the split occupation and nothing more. By accepting those terms there is at least something we will gain from this diplomatic encounter.

Option two is to just straight up deny the deal. Negotiations are very likely to break down as a result of this action, but it sends a message to the Republic. If they are not willing to accept our terms, then there will be no deal made with them.

The last option is to change the proposal so it is more favorable for the Republic, making them more inclined to accept it. This can be achieved by allowing Republican companies to operate in our part of Valencia. This gesture of reciprocity should be enough to win over the Republicans. However there are some that fear this could end up being worse for us as this would allow Republican companies to dominate in our part, while our companies would struggle to break through in their part.

options.name: Accepting the original deal is the safest bet.
Our terms were clear, the deal will be denied.
Let's alter our proposal and see if it will change their minds.

title: Catalonian persistence
desc:
The Catalonians are not ready to give up just yet. They have sweetened the deal by changing it so that now our businesses would also be allowed to operate in their part of Valencia. This gesture of reciprocity is very welcome and makes the deal a lot fairer. Most are ready to accept their additional proposal as it would benefit both of our economies,improving our relations with the Catalonians at a time when allies are few and enemies plenty.

However, there remains a group which still does not want any form of economic agreement with Catalonia and leave the issue a matter of occupation. They proclaim the danger of indirectly funding separatism and this economic agreement may only bankroll future issues. Furthermore they want to send a message to the Catalan government. Our proposal was final. The constant Catalan meddling is not welcome and will not be tolerated. This firm stance will certainly prevent the Catalonians from attempting to take advantage of our generosity, but it might stress the relations with one of our few allies. Something we cannot afford right now.

options.name: This seems like a fair proposal, sign it.
The original deal is the only option, nothing else.

title: The Spanish Refuse Free Cross-Border Trade
desc:
Despite our best efforts to compromise, allowing businesses to operate across both occupation zones, their delegation has returned a negative answer: our businesses in their zone will be treated as foreign businesses.

This is a hard pill to swallow for many in our delegation, but many have already voiced that the time to ratify has come. The Spanish have made it clear that we will not be able to extract any further concessions from them and the agreement is simply too important to let go over the issue of tariffs. A Spanish government recognizing our sovereignty, even over a part of Valencia, will be too large of a diplomatic coup to pass up even if trading with the other part will be more difficult than we had hoped.

On the other hand, some delegates claim that this outright refusal by the Spanish shows clearly that they never intended to negotiate with us in good faith. They say that the Spanish have made it clear that they will never truly bring themselves to accept the loss of "their" territory. That they will attempt to use any coercive measures to force us back into the fold and accept their oversight. For now these may be economic measures, but after the war with the fascists ends? Their questions hang over many in our delegation.

options.name: Not the results we had hoped for, but this is acceptable.
We will not let the Spanish corner us, neither economically nor militarily.

title: The Spanish Demand to Occupy all of Valencia
desc:
When the Spanish agreed to sit at the negotiation table with us, many expected them to drive as hard of a bargain as possible. As such, they were not surprised when the Spanish delegation reached out to us with their first demand: the complete withdrawal Catalan forces from Valencia and allowing them to occupy the entire region for the duration of the War.

Our delegation finds itself in a difficult position. While many delegates are hesitant to accept these maximalist demands, some demand more hawkish positions than others. Hawks say that we cannot allow ourselves to be taken advantage of by the Spanish. That we have fought with the blood of our soldiers, not theirs: it cannot have been spilled for nothing. These delegates say we must demand at least a split occupation of the region, and to make it clear that we intend to withdraw from the negotiations if that demand is not accepted.

Some members are more pragmatic. They claim that we need to have the Republic on our side both during the War and after it unless we and the rest of the Galeusca nations wish to be picked off one by one. Occupying even half of Valencia would require manpower, resources and Spanish goodwill which would be better spent securing ourselves. Letting the Spanish expend their limited resources, and thanking us for the opportunity to do so, would allow us to conserve our forces and end the war with a better bargaining position.

However, all remain wary of the maximalist Spanish attitude and do not propose that we blindly trust them to hold up their end of the bargain. They propose that if we are to accept the Spanish occupying all of Valencia, they must be made to accept a Galeusca contribution to their occupation forces. Not only will this make the Spanish occupation more palatable to the public, it will allow the Republic's 'precious allies' to keep an eye on them.

options.name: The Galeusca alliance will hold the Spanish to their word.
We can't have the Spanish tear our lands apart!

title: The Catalans Demand a Split Occupation
desc:
The Catalan delegation has returned to us after consulting Barcelona. Their answer is firm: Catalan soldiers died to liberate Valencia and the Catalan people still have a role to play there. They're threatening not to recognize any unilateral Spanish occupation of Valencian territory, risking the military cooperation provided for by the terms of the Anti-Fascist Cooperation Pact.

Our delegates are understandably frustrated, but split on the proper response. Many believe that we should hold firm. After all, the Catalans would be near helpless without the Pact and - hopefully - they will realize this. They will have to understand that the Pact is more important to their ultimate survival than a sliver of Spanish territory. Their stance is clear: with our superior manpower, material and legitimacy we are simply far better suited to taking the strain of such an occupation while they focus on maintaining their own smaller forces, and in doing so prevent the spread of further ideas of secession Catalonia may try to foment.

However, others call for a more conciliatory approach. Splitting the occupation might be unpopular among hawkish members of our government and public but it will help us to cement our image as a dependable, peaceful ally. It may even help prevent future friction in Iberia once the War is over and, while it is true that our resources are greater than Barcelona's, we do not possess so much as to disregard such opportunities to ensure more of it goes to the frontlines. Our magnanimity, they claim, will be richly rewarded in the long term by having the Catalans effectively subsidise our war effort, putting us in a stronger diplomatic and military position once peace returns.

options.name: Catalonia is brave, but not responsible for Valencia.
We cannot deny the chance for both peace and profit.

title: To Be Governed
desc:
Our delegation's efforts have borne fruit. After initially demanding our forces withdraw from Valencia, we have now been informed that the Spanish are willing to commit to a split occupation and close the matter. All that is left for us to do is to formalize the agreement and end the negotiations.

The mood has been positive, our tenacious negotiators having managed to drive a hard bargain and asserting ourselves to the Spanish. They will now publicly show us to be equals, a victory not just for our Republic but all the peoples of Iberia, and the door to Valencian self-determination lies open. While there are some issues to be sorted out - border control, security cooperation, trade restrictions and the like - these are trifling details that can be discussed at a later date once the agreement itself is signed.

There remains dissent however. Some members of our delegation continue to warn against Spaniards bearing gifts, pointing out Spain's stern stance from the start. They say that the Spanish are making us accept a lesser deal while having us believe we have taken a lot. That we are being taken for fools. Despite the loss of Valencia, they argue that we must walk away from the deal to demonstrate that Catalonia cannot be manipulated through minor concessions. How will the Spanish conduct themselves in future knowing that they can easily make us think mere recognition of proper status-quos are somehow great victories? The view of this small but vocal group is clear: strength against Spain requires wisdom, and here is a true test of the Republic's.

options.name: Victory! Approve the deal, with three cheers to our diplomats!
Sometimes, defeat is so nefarious that it dresses as victory. Reject the deal.

title: The Spanish Refuse to Split the Occupation
desc:
It seems that our delegation's firm answer to the Spanish has been met by an equally firm response. The Spanish claim that their recognition of the Catalan government as legitimate only extends to the areas controlled by us when the Cooperation Pact was signed; that any further territory our forces take is rightfully and solely Spanish. While they do make note of and thank Catalan bravery in the liberation, they demand that we withdraw our forces from Valencia and have made it clear that they will not discuss the issue any further.

Indeed, it seems that there is no more room for discussion. Many members of our delegation, furious at the apparent Spanish willingness to shed Catalan blood only to expand their own control, are prepared to walk out of the negotiations. They proclaim that there can be no recognition of the Spanish occupation of Catalan lands and no cooperation with the Spanish government, having proven itself to be untrustworthy, while it lasts.

Some of our delegates, however, dispute this rage. While they too bristle at the Spanish rejection, they highlight that the justification given isn't entirely unreasonable under the terms of the Pact. Certainly not enough to disregard it. That Catalan independence, even if maimed by the lack of Valencia, is better than subjugation and the issue should have been pressed during the signing of the Pact itself. As no acknowledgement of the Catalan claim to Valencia had been drawn, is it really wise to spite the Spanish over it now? Despite the patriotic furore roused in the delegation by the Spanish rejection, these delegates warn that we simply cannot take on the Fascists alone.

options.name: The Spanish can call it what they like, we recognise the stab in the back.
Through gritted teeth, we must agree.

title: The Catalans demand Galeusca Monitoring Mission
desc:
The Catalan delegation has agreed to our full occupation of Valencia, thankfully. While understandably unhappy they have requested a concession in order to soften the news to the Catalan public. They tell us that the Catalan public have developed a keen interest in the region; a desire to safeguard it from the return of repression, seeing it as a microcosm of the war as a whole. If we will not split the occupation, the Catalans ask that our occupation of the territory receive a Galeusca contribution.

Many delegates see this as an unnecessary but harmless concession to help us rebuild bridges after straining them by refusing Catalonia. While doubts about the authenticity of the justification remain, and the fact this is transparently a monitoring mission dressed in humility, the limited nature of the request and the free resources it offers us are enough to give most pause. Not to mention the sigh of relief this will give our diplomats.

However, it has been pointed out that the Basques and Galicians, as allies of the Catalan government, are inherently biased toward it and are unsuitable to contribute to our occupation. As aspects of the operation will be staffed by them, who under the deal will be operating in their own detachments, it could easily become a tool to undermine our occupation and foster Catalan influence under our nose. Their reach can be limited but we cannot watch these units constantly. Given the already demonstrated Catalan aggression directed at Valencia we cannot rule out intentions of foul play.

A compromise candidate, the Red Cross, has been floated as a neutral party to ease Barcelona's mind as to the conduct of our occupation. If accepted, they will oversee our political efforts, reconstruction and occupation policies and freely report them. After all, if their only interest is fair treatment then on what grounds can Barcelona oppose?

options.name: Free resources and diplomatic goodwill? Approve the Galeusca contributions.
An impartial body to reassure our allies should ease minds, suggest the Red Cross.
They try to seize our land, now they want their friends in our blind spots? No deal.

title: What about the Red Cross?
desc:
The Republic hasn't outright denied our request for some form of oversight in the region, which is a good sign. However, it's still not the answer we were hoping for. They have stated that such a Galeusca contribution could potentially bias parts of their occupation towards "minor but divisive local political movements" and could lead to instability, something they have suggested we'd surely want to avoid given our war.

As such, the Red Cross has been suggested to support their occupation instead.Some of the delegates have praised the merits of the Spanish plan, stating that while it's not ideal, the Red Cross offers a way to keep an eye on the Spanish in the region and force them to admit they can no longer act in a completely unilateral way there in future. Such a seed, while appearing minor, is just what we need to maintain Spanish acknowledgement of causes such as ours.

However, this would eliminate most of our direct influence over the region. Therefore, many have voiced their opposition to such a settlement. We have already agreed to retreat from Valencia and have been more than reasonable in the negotiations. The Red Cross lacks the ability to assert itself the way a Galeusca contribution would and, as a non-combatant force, can be easily misdirected by the Spanish. Resultingly this 'concession' may well be little more than a thin mask for total Spanish subjugation of the region.This, it is argued, would be little more than an exploitation of our good faith.

options.name: The Red Cross will do fine.
No half measures.

title: Nothing, Not Even a Glimpse
desc:
The Spanish response has been simple, but final. While regretting the political implications of Valencia being returned to Spain, they state that they cannot risk the stability of a Spanish region for little reason other than foreign newspaper headlines. A Galeusca contingent carries risk of frustrating the local political situation as well as distracting from the war effort of all in the Pact. They have made it clear: the occupation and rebuilding of Valencia will be a solely Spanish affair.

Emotions have run high at this development, many having hoped for a compromise, and now the delegation finds itself split. While embarrassed by the Spanish refusal of their compromise, the more cooperation-motivated delegates still advocate simply accepting the situation and officialising the withdrawal. They highlight that our continued presence in Valencia will face building difficulties without legitimacy, and we do not have the resources to be frivolous.

While our commitment to checking Spanish imperialism and fostering self-determination is without question, embroiling us in a protracted occupation without Republican support while waging war elsewhere may be a recipe for disaster, helping no one. Their call is clear: we must pick our battles.

Across from them, however, there is growing sympathy with those advocating for a maximalist stance of our own. We fight for self-determination across Iberia, and if the Spanish will stand in its way, then why should we go along with it? After all, every Catalan, Galician, or Euskadian who has fought and died thus far was one less of theirs who had to. To continue to disregard this and ignore the importance of the Galeusca cause shows the Republicans still haven't learned and don't value us as equals. The only option to maintain our position as an advocate of anti-imperialism, according to these delegates, is to walk away from the negotiations, leaving nothing signed. If the Spanish will not budge, then neither should we.

options.name: Knowing when to fight and when to retreat determines ultimate victory. Sign on the dotted line.
Our resolve is stronger than Spanish bluster. We won't dignify it with a signature.
The ink is still wet.
The ink is still wet.
Somewhere, a receiver is smashed against a wall.
No questions, thank you.

title: An Unholy Alliance
desc:
They stood around a table, an older oak creation brought in from a meeting room just as the civil war began. A creased map of Iberia was laid out, dotted pins marking the location of divisions with yellow strings marking the frontlines. The men stood, their thoughts filled with war.

"Unfortunately, issues surrounding availability of trained soldiers have persisted." said Brigadier General Alejandro Obrero, looking at the map in front of him with concern. "Militia and local conscripts plug gaps, but we will struggle to move forward without trained men. If we concentrate them we risk a collapse if we're attacked elsewhere."

"Indeed." responded Colonel Conejero, grabbing a pencil and pointing it toward a gap in the Junta's string. "This gap could very well be pivotal in advancing; we need to attack before it can be closed."

Obrero nodded, musing. "The Junta is not fated to be strong." His eyes flicked over Galicia, Catalonia and the Basque. "They're overstretched, fighting on numerous fronts with separatists and are struggling to quash partisans. We could gamble on an offensive."

Brigadier General Lago looked again at the front, stroking his chin in thought, lifting it as he spoke. "But risk our frontline in the process. Perhaps... we could ally with those separatists?" A few generals lifted their eyebrows, out of curiosity more than rejection. "If we coordinate, the force multiplier could allow us to move our soldiers where we need them without fearing counter-attack elsewhere. A multiple front offensive would guarantee us the initiative."

Obrero frowned, struggling to find an alternative. "Possibly," he replied begrudgingly, "but we can't advance such a proposal unilaterally."

options.name: And so, the notion was kicked down the road by a few days more.

title: Coalition of the Willing?
desc:
It was late in the day, the sunset filtering in through a window obscured by a series of dark grey clouds. Torcuato Fernandez-Miranda buried his head for a moment. Suggestions of a potential alliance with the separatist republics had circulated in a handful of meetings, but had been advanced with only the deepest caution and, admittedly, delayed as long as they could.

"If we go ahead with this plan, then we have to be careful." said Pío Canabillas, looking at the notes in front of him with suspicion. "Catalonia in particular might pressure us to move out of Valencia. These are people who see little difference between us and Franco."

José Maldonado sighed as he read through, shaking his head at both the prospect and comments. "All of them will believe that any Spanish government, fascist or democratic, would seek reintegration by any means necessary."

"So, we should recognise their independence?" asked Fernandez-Miranda, his voice growing quieter, more downtrodden. "After all, unless we prevail there's a Sword of Damocles over us all, separatist or not. Let's be candid, does this help us win the War?"

José Miguel Vega Rodríguez leant forwards. "My officers all agree it would benefit us, allowing us to better allocate men and resources." He shrugged. "We would have a better idea where their soldiers are and, overly simplified, can count on more men to attack them."

Nodding at the comment but maintaining a blank expression, Maldonado cleared his throat to interject. "If there's no opposition to this, I'll propose a cooperation pact as soon as we establish regular contact with them."

options.name: Let us only hope that this isn't a truly Faustian bargain.

title: Cooperation Pact - Basque Response
desc:
FROM: Ministry of Foreign Affairs

TO: Prime Minister Torcuato Fernandez-Miranda

TOPIC: Negotiations with the Republic of Euskadi

CLASSIFIED

Efforts to establish relations with the Republic of Euskadi have faced numerous difficulties. Established phone lines between Seville and Bilbao have long since been cut, and any links remaining have to rely on either connections through France, which remains relatively hostile to Basque independence, or Galicia. In order to establish firm communications, a mixture of both have been used, though greater priority has been placed on strengthening contact links through Galicia, which will likely remain more reliable.

The Republic of Euskadi is the most established of the separatists, but there are still internal concerns. Although there is staunch support for independence within the Basque Country itself, Navarra is much more split, with a much larger Spanish population and a higher proportion of supporters for the Junta who fear reprisal. Meanwhile, the government is internally split between right-wing and left-wing nationalists, and would likely buckle without the unifying presence of Lehendakari Telesforo Monzón.

Despite this, there is general interest in forging an anti-Fascist Cooperation Pact. Beyond general demands for recognition and general caution in negotiating with a Spanish government, there doesn't seem to be much opposition to the formation of an alliance. Though they requested the opportunity to have broader meetings on the issue, Monzón has rejected any firm commitments until being able to contact Tarradellas and Velo about the issue. We will likely have to take their views into account as well.

options.name: - José Maldonado

title: A Deal with the Devil? - To Vigo
desc:
Xose Vélo looked down at the receiver in front of him, a strangely shaped and triangular device, as he cradled a phone in one hand. Discussions between his government and the Republican Spanish government in Seville had been ongoing for the past few days and he had been approached with a deal. If Vélo was more naive, he wondered, he might have taken it at face value.

"Well, it's a good sign that Fernandez-Miranda is willing to approach us." said the voice of Tarradellas, garbled by distance and infrastructure. "We shouldn't treat this as unworthy of our backing."

Vélo frowned as he heard the comments. "Of course, this is a positive step, but there's a lot further for him to go." A few aides passed by him, placing down brief memos on the movement of Junta troops. "I agree with this in principle; a strong Republic could help end the war quicker, and to keep it a strictly Spanish affair. It could be the only way for us to survive during the war, but beyond it? How can we trust they don't view us as junior partners? It's only going to hurt our claims to independence in the long-term."

A period of silence followed, but was subsumed as Tarradellas finally replied. "I do understand those concerns." The voice sounded slightly quieter than before, and occasional noise filtered through in the form of targeted static. "Perhaps it could work if we officially make our demands unilateral through the formation of a direct political alliance?"

Another voice crackled into barely audible life, this time from Telesforo Monzón. "That would be a wise move. Our ties are already strong enough, and already allow for some coordination. We must be assertive in such a position, and push the Republic into officially recognising us as independent before we sign any such pact." Velo considered the measure for a moment, but only long enough to fully consider the consequences before agreeing.

options.name: The die is cast.

title: Cooperation Pact - Catalan Response
desc:
FROM: Ministry of Foreign Affairs

TO: Prime Minister Torcuato Fernandez-Miranda

TOPIC: Negotiations with the Galician Republic

CLASSIFIED

Efforts to establish communications with the Catalan capital of Barcelona were made with little difficulty. Although there is still some distance in our frontlines, the Junta having cut existing phone lines between Seville and Barcelona, the Baleares have remained a viable alternative that whilst not completely without flaw, have remained mostly reliable. There may be some risk of the line being cut should naval activity resurge or become targeted, but that is unlikely at the present time.

Catalonia has some issues internally. Support for independence is very high, but the war cabinet was only formed at the last minute. It seems to be mostly functional, with a broadly, but not entirely left-wing outlook, but the long period of exile for many has hampered the popularity of the government, and its abilities to adapt to pressures within Catalonia, both relating to social issues and to the issue of Pancatalanism.

Overall, efforts to forge an Anti-Fascist Cooperation Pact are fruitful, but have come up short. The issue of Pancatalanism, and of annexing both Valencia and the Baleares has decreased overall interest in forming a public alliance, but overall support remains nonetheless, even if only whilst the Junta remains an active factor. Though they requested the opportunity to have broader meetings on the issue, Velo has rejected any firm commitments until being able to contact Tarradellas and Monzón about the issue. We will likely have to take their views into account as well.

options.name: - José Maldonado

title: A Deal with the Devil? - To Barcelona
desc:
Josep Tarradellas looked at the three-pronged device in front of him, a receiver dedicated to staging conference calls. Since Catalonia had received its independence, it had become a constant, discussions with the other separatist republics punctuated by negotiations with cabinet ministers split on the issue of Pancatalanism. Discussions between his government and the Republican Spanish government in Seville had been ongoing for the past few days, and he had been approached with a deal.

"Well, it's a good sign that Fernandez-Miranda is willing to approach us." he said, looking around as a few aides passed him. With how divided his cabinet was, he didn't want to risk making any firm moves on a deal. "We shouldn't treat this as unworthy of our backing."

"Of course, this is a positive step, but there's a lot further for him to go." protested Xosé Velo, his line sputtering to life through a dense haze of static. I agree with this in principle; a strong Republic could help end the war quicker, and to keep it a strictly Spanish affair. It could be the only way for us to survive during the war, but beyond it? How can we trust they don't view us as junior partners? It's only going to hurt our claims to independence in the long-term."

Tarradellas struggled to set the assertion aside. Galicia's position was particularly tenuous, but he could not ignore the risk that Galician integration would only serve as precedent for integrating the other two separatists. As the final aide left, he lifted the phone from his ear as he asked her to stop others from entering. "I do understand those concerns. Perhaps it could work if we officially make our demands unilateral through the formation of a direct political alliance?"

The voice of Telesforo Monzón came to life, garbled though it was. "That would be a wise move. Our ties are already strong enough, and already allow for some coordination. We must be assertive in such a position, and push the Republic into officially recognising us as independent before we sign any such pact." Tarradellas considered the proposal, and then smiled as he came to accept it.

options.name: The die is cast.

title: Cooperation Pact - Galician Response
desc:
FROM: Ministry of Foreign Affairs

TO: Prime Minister Torcuato Fernandez-Miranda

TOPIC: Negotiations with the Galician Republic

CLASSIFIED

Efforts to establish contact with the Republic of Galicia were relatively difficult but have succeeded. The distance between our territory and that of the Galician capital in Vigo necessitates the use of telephone connections within Portugal. Most existing telephone connections go through the territory of the Junta, and have already been cut. That being said, those existing lines in Portugal are functional, and should remain as such for the foreseeable future.

The Galician Republic seems to have some difficulty with legitimacy. Although large portions of the population remain steadfast in opposing Franco, there seems to be less interest in forming an independent Galician state and the government that does exist was only formed at the last minute. This may provide some difficulty for it to resist pressure from the Junta, but such issues will likely be resolved by specifically focusing a joint coalition's message as being anti-fascist.

Overall, efforts to forge an Anti-Fascist Cooperation Pact are fruitful, but have come up short. Beyond rallying support within Galicia, exploiting a major weakness in the frontlines of the Junta is a prospect that Prime Minister Xosé Velo and Councillor Ramón Otero Pedrayo seem to be particularly interested in. However, although they requested the opportunity to have broader meetings on the issue, Velo has rejected any firm commitments until being able to contact Tarradellas and Monzón about the issue. We will likely have to take their views into account as well.

options.name: - José Maldonado

title: A Deal with the Devil? - To Vigo
desc:
Xose Vélo looked down at the receiver in front of him, a strangely shaped and triangular device, as he cradled a phone in one hand. Discussions between his government and the Republican Spanish government in Seville had been ongoing for the past few days and he had been approached with a deal. If Vélo was more naive, he wondered, he might have taken it at face value.

"Well, it's a good sign that Fernandez-Miranda is willing to approach us." said the voice of Tarradellas, garbled by distance and infrastructure. "We shouldn't treat this as unworthy of our backing."

Vélo frowned as he heard the comments. "Of course, this is a positive step, but there's a lot further for him to go." A few aides passed by him, placing down brief memos on the movement of Junta troops. "I agree with this in principle; a strong Republic could help end the war quicker, and to keep it a strictly Spanish affair. It could be the only way for us to survive during the war, but beyond it? How can we trust they don't view us as junior partners? It's only going to hurt our claims to independence in the long-term."

A period of silence followed, but was subsumed as Tarradellas finally replied. "I do understand those concerns." The voice sounded slightly quieter than before, and occasional noise filtered through in the form of targeted static. "Perhaps it could work if we officially make our demands unilateral through the formation of a direct political alliance?"

Another voice crackled into barely audible life, this time from Telesforo Monzón. "That would be a wise move. Our ties are already strong enough, and already allow for some coordination. We must be assertive in such a position, and push the Republic into officially recognising us as independent before we sign any such pact." Velo considered the measure for a moment, but only long enough to fully consider the consequences before agreeing.

options.name: The die is cast.

title: Galeusca
desc:
Xosé Velo sat in his sunlit office, face covered in makeup with cameras and microphones crowding out his desk and cabinets. This was their only chance. A bit of discomfort was tolerable in the pursuit of freedom.

"Men and women of Galicia. I am addressing you today to proclaim a new, noble alliance of the long-oppressed peoples of Iberia. The Union is no more and the governments of Spain and Portugal are in disarray. As Galicians, this is our opportunity to seize our place in the family of free peoples, along with our Catalan and Basque compatriots."

Josep Tarradellas stood in front of the assembled quorum in the richly decorated hall of the Palace of Parliament, proudly preparing to reveal one of his greatest achievements since independence.

"Esteemed members! We never faltered in our commitment to freedom and national self-determination for Catalunya, even during the darkest oppression and despair. However, we are a small nation; our backs to the sea and a foe that is still determined to see us subjugated once and for all. So, we have decided to unite with the newly liberated peoples of Iberia in a military alliance. I am certain that with our combined might, we will assert ourselves as beacons of hope for all oppressed peoples."

Telesforo Monzón stood on a large podium in Bilbao, addressing the crowds with tears in his eyes. This was not 1936 anymore. So many were gone. But sometimes, he reckoned, life is kind enough to give a second chance. "Basques! We were the first to rise up, after so many years of tyranny. We haven't forgotten the martyrs of the first civil war, and now we have another chance. A chance to avenge them; make the dream they died for reality. We welcome any of the free people of Iberia to aid us in our struggle, to make this land that so many have died for into one worth living for."

options.name: Three nations, one hope.

title: Cutting off the Gangrenous Limb
desc:
Foreign Minister José Maldonado closed the door behind him, clearly flustered. He shook his head, stood up straight, and walked to the Cabinet table. All eyes were fixed on him. "Apologies, gentlemen. Busy day."

President Fernandez quietly gestured for Maldonado to take his seat, before addressing the table. "Gentlemen, as stated in the summons, we need to discuss our response to the alliance between the Basque, Catalan and Galician republics. I trust you have all considered potential positions? This is a development we cannot leave unanswered. Señor Maldonado has requested an opportunity to put some further considerations before us before we continue."

Maldonado sighed and took out his notes, muttering under his breath before finding the right page. "Let us not mince words here: this decision by the breakaway governments has put us in quite the difficult spot. We are supposed to save Spain, not dismember it. Furthermore, this agreement also means that we can't sign separate pacts with the governments - it's recognizing all three or falling out with them all. This means they will be able to demand more of us, as they now represent a sizable unified force. This wedge may... complicate the undertaking of the Anti-Fascist Cooperation Pact."

Fernandez nodded quietly, before turning to Defense Minister José Rodríguez. "Your thoughts, General?"

Rodríguez immediately began talking, as if concerned someone might try to sneak in an argument before him. "With all due respect, President Fernandez, this is too important for us to throw aside. Politics can come later - for now, military necessity must be prioritized. That necessity is to sign the AFCP, even if that means recognition. We need to bolster our forces, and they know they can't defeat the fascists without us;that they will lose everything by losing this alliance. We have to maintain the negotiations."

options.name: The council slowly agreed.

title: Trapped with Each Other
desc:
The cabinet meeting next morning was no less contentious. A decision on the recognition of the regional governments had not been reached; time was running out to lock down a valuable alliance - or so one side of the room claimed. Many others saw little but dismemberment of Spain, a faustian bargain.

Maldonado leaned forward, sighing as he again waved the papers in his hand. "Our counterparts in the governing structures of the breakaway regions have made it quite clear that no alliance with our government is possible without our recognition of their legitimacy. They demand their national rights be vindicated and that we commit to respecting them as sovereign governments".

President Fernández sighed and nodded, glaring at the ministers. "This has gone in circles too long. We need a decision." All eyed each other. None wished to repeat yesterday's argument, but such verbal carnage seemed inevitable. Arguments began to creep into their throats once more.

"I have an idea - it's not perfect, but it might be our best option".

All eyes turned to Vice-President Cabanillas as he rose from his seat. "In this war, we need any advantage we can get. Bolstering our forces and extending our enemy's line is just that, but we can't be pushovers. So, when is a promise not a promise? We differentiate legitimacy and independence. We recognize them as legitimate administrations but leave the question of independence for after the war, when we can discuss the condition of Spain properly. The people now are frightened, our nation is in chaos and we have all heard the stories of the barbarity being committed by our enemies. The people should consider such a question only when peace returns and they aren't subjected to regionalist slogans playing on their fears. As for the separatists? They may not like it, but they'll know that this is the best chance they'll have."

options.name: One by one, the ministers nodded.

title: The Spanish Counteroffer
desc:
Velo reached gingerly for the phone. He had waited for this call for a few days, but the mere idea of negotiations with the Spanish government was unnerving. As necessary as it was, signing an agreement with the imperialists made his stomach churn. But, it had to be done.

"Señor Fernández?" Velo answered as nonchalantly as he could. He would not give the Spanish leader the satisfaction of addressing him as President. Recognition would have to be mutual.

"Señor Velo. The Spanish Republic has taken note of your alliance with the other separatist regions. Out of a desire to maintain good relations across the peninsula and with an eye to possible military cooperation, the government proposes the following..." Fernandez sounded like he was reading off a script. Perhaps he was. Velo bristled at some of the terms used, but official talk was official talk- it helped Velo restrain the disdain that burned at every half spoken implication or euphemism. Velo swallowed his response and waited.

"We offer to recognize the governing authorities of the three regions as separate governments, whose exact relationship with the Spanish Republic will be determined by popular referendums after the victorious conclusion of the War. While it lasts, the Spanish government will endeavor towards cooperation, for the better prosecution of the war effort." Fernandez's voice seemed to darken, "I think we are both aware of the alternative in this war. Is this agreeable to you?"

Velo paused, the question hanging over the phone line. The Galeusca alliance had demanded immediate recognition of independence and he didn't trust the Spanish to hold their side of the bargain, especially as the war ended. But did they really have a choice? This was likely the best offer they were going to get, and if the alternative was to fight the fascists alone...

options.name: "You hold up your end Spaniard, and we'll hold up ours. We'll be watching."

title: The Spanish Counteroffer
desc:
Monzón reached out for the phone. The idea of negotiating with the Spanish for Euskadi's independence left a bitter taste in his mouth but this was too important. He gripped the receiver tightly. "President Fernández?"

"Señor Monzón-" The Spanish President began, before his counterpart interjected. "You mean President Monzón. We negotiate as equals or not at all."

The voice was silent for a moment. "...Yes. I was intending to let you know that the Spanish Republic has taken note of your alliance with the... leaders of the Catalan and Galician regions. We wish to maintain cordial relations with all of you and cooperate against the fascists and, because of that, we have a proposition for you."

Monzón could hear the condescension in the Spaniard's voice. Typical Spanish arrogance. Thinking that they could just enforce terms on his people's very existence. But, he had to admit, his people's very existence was at stake here. His knuckles whitened around the receiver as he mustered every bit of his diplomatic skill. "Go on"

."We propose recognizing your governing authorities as separate governments, whose exact relationship to us will be determined by popular referendums after the war-"

Monzón interjected once more. "How can we trust that you won't just take us over once the war is over? How can we trust that this referendum will even take place, or that you won't rig it? I'll put it simply - I don't trust you."

"You don't have to cooperate," the voice on the other side stiffened. "Go alone if you want. But then it's you, surrounded on all sides, with no one to help you. I know who I'd take my chances with if I were you. This doesn't have to be about trust."

options.name: Monzón frowned. "Tell me more about that cooperation you mentioned."

title: The Spanish Counteroffer
desc:
Tarradellas reached for the phone. This call was a few days in the making, but he had already made up his mind. He was not going to betray Catalan interests to the Spanish but this agreement was, all things considered, a Catalan interest. "President Fernández?"

"Señor Tarradellas, it is good to speak with you." Tarradellas' frowned slightly at not being referred to as President, but he let it slide. This agreement was more important than his title. These things could wait for after the war. "The Government of the Spanish Republic has taken note of your alliance with the other separatist regions. We'd like to maintain cordial relations across the peninsula, and cooperate against the fascists, in whom we have a shared enemy. In order to facilitate that, we have a proposition for you."

Tarradellas noted his counterpart's tone, formal but rather relaxed. He could imagine that his conversations with the Basque and Galician leaders were more stressful and was happy to be the voice of reason in these circumstances.

Fernandez continued. "We offer to recognize the governing authorities of the three regions as separate governments, whose exact relationship with us will be determined by popular referendums after we win the War. Until then, we'll make sure to concretely cooperate with these governments and make sure we do, in fact, win. What do you think?"

Tarradellas leaned back in his chair. Velo and Monzon would no doubt have gritted teeth over this, but to him this sounded quite reasonable. With their back to the sea, the Catalan government was in no position to refuse a hand offered in help, particularly if it was counterbalanced by the Galeusca agreement. If this was the best they were going to get, he thought, Catalonia could definitely live with that.

options.name: "I think that sounds quite reasonable, Señor Fernández."

title: Cooperation, if You Can Keep it
desc:
SEVILLA. - President of the Spanish Republic Torcuato Fernández-Miranda has today signed the Anti-Fascist Cooperation Pact, heralding a new era of cooperation with the Basque, Catalan, and Galician regions. Speaking to reporters in the Provisional Government Palace, his excellency proclaimed that the prospects of a quick and victorious conclusion to the war have now dramatically increased, as well as those of a peaceful resolution of the national question in Iberia afterwards...

BILBAO. - ...In a speech after signing the pact, Xosé Velo has touted the agreement as necessary in the face of fascist aggression, expressing his hope that it will help cement the freedom the people of Galicia have regained after so long, along with that of the other liberated nations on the peninsula. He has also stated that, while the Spanish have promised to cooperate militarily and politically during the war and after it, it is his mission to make sure that the Galician resistance, in collaboration with Catalonia and the Basque Country, hold them to that promise...

BARCELONA. - ...Speaking to the press after the fact, President Tarradellas proclaimed: "Today, we have truly taken our place among the family of peoples. This agreement will aid us in defeating the fascists who wish to swallow us once more, and help bring forth an era of friendly relations among the peoples of Iberia, one where we are treated on an equal footing..."

VIGO. - ...In a radio and television broadcast following the ceremony, President Monzón addressed the Basque nation, remarking: "This pact marks a significant step in our rise as a true people, no longer the lapdogs of foreign conquerors but a sovereign people whose fate is determined by itself alone". He has also claimed that while this agreement is an important milestone, it is not the end of the struggle: the war must be fought to a successful conclusion and the liberated peoples of Iberia must hold the Republican Spanish government to its word, with all of the means at their disposal...

options.name: Perhaps diplomacy isn't dead.

title: Падение Жироны
desc:
Только звук тяжелого дыхания раздавался в темноте подвала.

Несколькими днями ранее они были пленниками Народной армии. Они совершили ошибку, слишком открыто заявив о своем неприятии социализма в первые дни войны, будь то по политическим или моральным мотивам. В комнате находились люди, которые нашли бы пристанище почти в каждой фракции Испании.

Совсем недавно их бросили в темноту. По какой причине? Что ж, они сами не были уверены. Их похитители сказали им вести себя тихо, и покорно ждать своей судьбы. С тех пор они только и делали, что слышали звуки шагов и глухие удары войны. Никто не пришел. В комнату никто не входил.

Через некоторое время люди решили начать действовать. Они на ощупь поднялись по ступенькам и попытались открыть дверь, но та не поддавалась. Они щупали стены, пытаясь найти выход, но все, что они нашли, была влажная водосточная труба. Они попытались понять, есть ли хоть какая-нибудь щель, откуда в комнату проникал бы воздух, но чернильная пустота не дала им ответов.

Измученные, все, что они могли делать, это сидеть и размышлять о своей судьбе - и что ж, именно это они и делали. Размышляли о своих прошлых ошибках. О сделанном выборе. Понимание того, что спасение лежало всего в нескольких метрах, было невыносимым. Тем, у кого были семьи и дети, пришлось еще хуже, поскольку они все больше понимали, что желание увидеть солнечный свет было куда больше, чем желание встретить своих собственных детей. В том подвале темнота таила в себе только сожаления и стыд.

Дышать становилось все тяжелее. При любом движении теперь можно было наткнуться на тела. Оставшиеся в живых знали, что большинство из них уже умерли. Теперь они просто сидели неподвижно, чувствуя, как пересыхает во рту, и сжимая окровавленные, ободранные от царапанья по двери и стенам, кончики пальцев. Они задавались вопросом, стоили ли их идеалы такой цены. Задавались вопросом, почему их похитители так и не вернулись.

options.name: Задавались вопросом, почему они должны были умереть.

title: Liberation of Girona
desc:
TOP SECRET

COMMUNIQUE TO THE WAR MINISTER: FOR IMMEDIATE ATTENTION

Sir

Girona has fallen, dealing a large blow to separatist strength in Northern Catalonia. Security forces are now beginning the slow process of preparing the city for post-separatist rule.There exist 4 notable obstacles

1: There is evidence many of the city's defenders, as well as a variety of citizens, fled into the mountains near the French border. Reports on their organization are contradictory but the basic fact seems clear.

2: Thanks to the prior described exodus, there remains strong paramilitary resistance in the North and West regions near the city. Safe transport via these routes is impossible.

3: Hostile elements remain in the city, but contained. Due to them using cultural landmarks as shields we do not wish to use overwhelming force.

4: Manpower shortages mean we cannot tackle the paramilitary problem as well as these sieges. As such firm attacks are recommended to free men for counter-terrorims action rather than protracted sieges.

The civilian population remains split, with dissidents still being present. Political prisons are being discovered in buildings, in some cases with the inhabitants already dead. Arrests are made as much as conditions allow, these found prisons being incorporated into our detainment resources, however we require clarification on the long term solution as our detainment centers approach overcrowding quickly.

General Carlos Fernandez, Head of Military Security District Catalonia.

options.name: Peace, with all its severity, returns to Girona.

title: Падение Толедо
desc:
Величественный Кафедральный собор Святой Марии в более мирные времена был известен своим готическим дизайном, который тонул в окружавшем его шуме. Каждый кашель, скрежет и шепот раздавались здесь с необычной громкостью.

Однако сегодня все эти звуки не были похожи на обычные мирные шорохи. Громкие раскаты взрывов проникали сквозь каменные стены. Верующие и неверующие - все они набились под своды собора. Войти в двери города означало шагнуть в ад, поскольку последняя бомбардировка превратила все, что они знали, в руины. Те, кто столпился внутри, надеялись, что Бог, либо крепкие стены собора, смогут их защитить.

У главного алтаря молились люди. Некоторые взрослые плакали, как дети. Некоторые просто сидели в ошеломленном молчании, не обращая внимания на нервные разговоры окружающих. Большое здание было освещено множеством свечей, благодаря большим запасам собора. Тусклый свет освещал золотые украшения и величественные арки. Частые вспышки сквозь витражи добавляли немного света, но мало помогали успокоить испуганных людей внизу. Вместо этого они молились, чтобы тусклый свет свечей стал единственным источником освещения.

Однако через несколько мгновений все закончилось. Собор сильно затрясся, пока всех людей внутри повалило на пол. Звуки взрыва, гораздо более громкие, чем предыдущие, повисли в воздухе. На мгновение все замерло. Затем раздался треск, отразившийся от старых камней. У немногих из находившихся внутри была возможность посмотреть вверх и увидеть, как некогда красивый потолок с громадной скоростью рушится на людей внизу.

options.name: Бог покинул Толедо.

title: Liberation of Toledo
desc:
TOP SECRET

COMMUNIQUE TO THE WAR MINISTER: FOR IMMEDIATE ATTENTION

Sir,

Toledo has been liberated from rebel control. Central Spanish position boosted as rebels have lost major logistical and defensive stronghold.

Urban rebel forces well prepared. Indirect fire tactics and shock offensives utilized. High amounts of organized and irregular combatants present.

Damage to the city is high. Assessments on available housing ongoing - projections suggest majority loss in high density areas. Civilian casualties high. Guerilla attacks persist. High number of displaced civilians complicating current military arrangements. Prisonersbeing documented. Identified prisoners of interest relocated for enhanced interrogations. Citizens and Prisoners being used in corpse disposal and other labor under supervision.

Request urgent delivery of artillery ammunition. Rear units required to set up monitored refugee facilities. Rations and medical equipment required to replace unexpected civilian expense.

General Fernando Cabrera, Head of Military Security District Center.

options.name: If the rebels should hide, we shall use our might to reveal them to our sun.

title: Падение Порту
desc:
До сих пор Айдену благоволила удача. Несмотря на то, что его призвали на войну, ему посчастливилось избежать худших боев, и он провел все свое время, выполняя бессмысленные патрули, скучные караульные обязанности и прочие малозначимые поручения. Бои за Порту мало чем отличались от его обычной рутины.

В его отряде были и другие жители Лиссабона. Томас, Даниэль, Эдуардо и Марко. Некоторые солдаты называли их негодяями, другие - торговцами товарами. Их запасом было все, что они находили. Этот навык был полезен во время войны, и их "способности" к добычи всего и вся позволяли им оказываться в безопасных и наживных местах. В конце концов, даже генералы не могли отказаться от легкой военной добычи, так почему бы не заключить неофициальное соглашение с солдатами, которое могло бы облегчить все это за разумную цену?

Сегодня они осматривали таинственный склад на окраине города. Эйден хотел проникнуть внутрь, но остальные не были уверены, стоило ли это затраченных усилий. Их громкие обсуждения прекратились, когда перед ними появился дряхлый старик с устаревшим дробовиком.

"Воры! Держитесь подальше от моего вина!" - закричал он и выстрелил. Отдача отбросила мужчину назад, и он застонал, когда оружие ударило ему прямо в хрупкое плечо. Выстрел пролетел над головами отряда, и они, не задумываясь, спокойно вскинули винтовки на плечо и застрелили пожилого мужчину.

"Итак, это вино. Нам на самом деле следовало бы знать, в конце концов, город славится этим продуктом. Должно быть, оно чрезвычайно хорошего качества, раз старый идиот был готов за него умереть."

Убедившись, что дело сделано, отряд начал выламывать дверь. Позже за ними приехали их друзья на грузовиках, и бочки с вином исчезли.

Старик же остался лежать там. Когда грузовики уехали, и увезли с собой последние намеки на жизнь, какое-то время украшавшая это здание, никто не удостоил его взглядом.

options.name: Бесславный конец неизвестной истории.

title: Освобождение Порту
desc:
Для Управления начальников штабов,

Джентльмены,

It is my pleasure to declare that Porto has been secured by our forces. As one of the largest cities within our nation, this victory represents a major step forward for the people of Portugal against the Monarchists due to its major role in the organization of the illegal monarchist movement in the North.

Its major urban character, industry and coastal location had made it vital for the monarchist economy. Due to land routes via Spain being closed off, it provided modest importing and exporting capability as well as a sizable population to serve in the King's armies. Through the expulsion of Monarchist forces we have deprived them of this vital resource.

Severe fighting took place in the outskirts and in some areas of the city near the coast during the initial advances, however a long urban campaign was fortunately prevented. Therefore the city is in mostly good condition with a feared humanitarian situation largely avoided. Local political figures have been detained, however most of the monarchist regime successfully fled, and PoWs are in the process of being relocated away from the city.

The population broadly is cautious, however firm ideological sentiment within the general population does not seem to be present, which has eased the transfer to our administration. While some accusations of illicit behavior by locals towards our troops have been recorded, most have been found to be fabrications while a small minority are in the process of being prosecuted. Further details will be communicated once the situation becomes clearer.

Signed,

Defence Minister Gomes

options.name: Long Live the King.

title: Fall of Aveiro
desc:
An uncharacteristically cold wind rattled Father Carlos as he stumbled through the rubble of what was once the old town of Aveiro. He muttered his prayers, holding tight to his rosary, as if to shield it - and himself - from the sharp whistle of the wind, carrying the sounds of shrieking bombs and forlorn screams. The ghosts of the old city had been disturbed, joined by a multitude of new lost souls torn from this earth by the fires of war.

Turning around a particularly large pile of rubble, which may once have been a building, Father Carlos gasped, reaching for his crucifix. In front of him, the moonlight cast a pale shadow over the ancient Cathedral of Aveiro, or at least, what was left of it. The Cathedral was established more than five hundred years ago, and has withstood the test of time, disasters, and regime change. But it could not stand against the destruction unleashed by war. Its shattered windows gazed at Father Carlos like horrified eyes, frozen in their last moments, and its spire stood at a precarious angle in front of him, a head cowering in submission.

Glass crunched under Father Carlos's boots as he staggered towards the ancient building, tears streaming down his face. At last, he leaned against the sagging walls, caressing the charred and pockmarked stones. He could now see empty casings and dark stains scattered across the ground, punctuated by the stark moonlight. A battle took place here, at a holy place, a sanctuary. Starkly opposing visions had led men to kill and die here, trampling the vision this place was meant to uphold. Father Carlos lifted his eyes to the cold light of the moon, wondering how many more sanctuaries of God would be desecrated by the senseless ideals that brought men to kill their own brethren.

options.name: The wind continued on, howling its anguish around him.

title: Aveiro's House of God
desc:
Trash Cans carrying fires were placed at intervals between beds around the room, casting a hazy medieval atmosphere on the once white walls.

The bins had been fed by the pews that had served the large hall, then anything wooden that could be torn away, but now the fuel was reduced to random trash. Flames dimly illuminated groaning wounded who writhed on beds stained from both their wounds and those of the departed. Orderlies dashed, carrying dishes overflowing with horrid liquids and tools stained red and black. Night had long since fallen, but no respite came.

The room stank. Aveiro Cathedral had lost its peace.

"To those inside this aid station, attention." A microphone from outside suddenly blared, pausing the flurry of activity for a moment. The orderlies and few doctors stopped, but the groans didn't. The voice from outside didn't care, talking over them.

"The Cathedral is surrounded by troops of the legitimate administration of Portugal." The few doctors began issuing orders to any who could walk. A pre-prepared bar was placed on the entrance, while the sparse supply crates by the altar were dragged into a rear room.

"Your army has left you; we control the city. All soldiers present are invited to surrender and prevent bloodshed. Exit the building with raised hands." The men and women on the beds moaned, asking what was happening. Some of those with less terrible wounds tried to stand, desperately throwing documents or clothing into the fires. They'd heard the rumors.

"Lethal force is authorized should you not." Militia soldiers entered the hall, pistols bared and taking position by pillars and behind beds, some still occupied.Their guns were trained on the entrance.

options.name: "Do not resist us."

title: Fall of Badajoz
desc:
The acrid smell that Javier had grown used to since the start of the war hung in the air, burning his nostrils. It was quiet, except for the dull hum of vehicles on the street below.

Javier sat slumped in a chair. The room he was in was an old apartment, bare after his unit had thrown most of the furniture out onto the street in days past. The windows were shattered, the walls and ceiling were covered in impact holes from bullets and ricochets. The walls were daubed, first with a monotone brown paint, next in scarlet blood.

Around the room were the remains of Javier's comrades. Some of them had been felled by bullets in the firefight, they had been lucky. It was quick. The others had pieces of their limbs around the room. A well placed couple of grenades had been lobbed into the rooms of the apartment, and the blasts had caught all but Javier. It had taken some time for them to slowly expire, and Javier had listened and watched every moment.

He had been lucky, one of his brother's bodies had absorbed the blast. He had been knocked into a wall but otherwise unhurt. Now he listened to the enemy pass by below, on their way to destroy his precious Spain, while he was slumped weakly in a corner.

He took out a picture of his wife - from a hiking trip a few years previous. She was sitting on a rock, looking up from a map. It had been a week-long trip, walking through rugged hills and woods completely disconnected from the world. There was only them. Her happy eyes and bright smile brought back the memories of that trip - the peace of the forests they had walked.

In his eyes, impotent tears welled.

options.name: To see her in this place...

title: Fall of Barcelona
desc:
"Have we got any flares down there, maybe we can spook 'em with that?"

"What?"

The tank commander grunted in exasperation and punched the metal of his temporary prison. It was cramped, the tank stunk and they had barely moved in two hours. He had been elated when Barcalona had been taken, but even with the terrorists running for the hills it seemed they just couldn't grasp that they were beaten.

"Sir?"

Below him his crew all looked at him, their wide doe eyes half his age awash with hesitation. They could barely hear each other over the roar, chanting and jeering from all directions that seemed to reverberate around the tank's interior. An earlier attempt to talk to the crowd had failed miserably, and some had even tried to open the hatch - something that a few placed shots had ended. Since then they had been locked in this standoff. They seemed satisfied to just chant slogans and block them.

"Castle 1 this is Castle 2, we have people trying to climb up on us again, we can't stay here! Over" came the radio, the gruff voice tinged with fear.

The tank commander weighed up his options. He couldn't stay here. Firing shots to disperse the crowd could backfire horribly; they didn't have much ammo and there were a hell of a lot of them. What to do?

He sighed, taking the radio receiver. "All units, this is Castle 1. Follow the leader. Out."

"But sir, the streets full, and there's barely anywhere for them to go. We'll run ov-"

"Drive."

options.name: Citizens avoided that road, for the smell hung in the air.

title: Fall of Barcelona
desc:
"The convoy is nearly over the bridge."

"Ok, be ready for my mark."

Lying in some scrub were a man and a woman, as close to the ground as possible and covered by tall grass. They were on a hill overlooking a highway, empty of the usual traffic that once marked the roads around Barcelona. Instead, a long convoy of military vehicles slowly drove along it.

The two had been part of the defense of the city they could see on the horizon, before that defense had utterly collapsed. They'd been forced to flee, but fortunately it was not an eventuality they were completely unprepared for. They had quickly relocated to one of their depots from before the war - explosives and small arms for use in the liberation of Catalonia, now to be used in its salvation.

The military convoy was made up mostly of trucks, while led and shadowed by some armored cars. Maybe they were carrying reinforcements? Ammunition or supplies for the occupiers? Neither of them cared. They were carrying something worth protecting, and that made it worth destroying.

The first armored car entered the bridge, but the mark didn't come. It made its way across, leading the convoy, until just before it left the cry came.

"Mark!"

With a button press the bridge vanished in a cloud of dust and debris, a handful of vehicles caught in the blast. It was loud, and the two saboteurs couldn't resist a whistle of triumph as they watched the remaining vehicles panic, driving off the road in all directions.

"That was for our people you sons of bitches!" they cried, before making their way off the hill and into the empty country.

options.name: Most of the food shipment was lost, as was an armored car.

title: Fall of Bilbao
desc:
"Stand in line, keep your hands behind your head. If you have a baby, hold them close to your chest and make no sudden moves. Do not face away from any military personnel or their advisors. Cooperation will be noted" the loudspeaker boomed, barely audible over the din.

It was the dark early hours of the morning, yet the estate was alive. Shouting, crying children, idling vehicles with their lights illuminating the area. Locals had stirred and stood behind the corden yelling and screaming. What they said could barely be made out individually, but the barbs of their glares said everything, eager to demonstrate their opposition against the criminals amongst them.

Behind the corden, a long line of people stood, perhaps 50 or 60 of many ages dragged from the apartments behind them. They had evidently been pulled from their beds, wearing little beyond underwear. Some unfortunate few wore nothing at all, but none of the soldiers cared for their shame. All shivered, either from cold or fear. Riflemen yelled that any movement meant death.

Amongst the chaos of uniforms, a small group of civilians consulted with officers. They walked down the line, pointing people out - those people then dragged away and thrown into a nearby truck. A child attempted to run after his parents, stopped by a rifle crack. None of the line dared move more.

They moved down the line, half of them being thrown into the waiting trucks. A loudspeaker announced the completion of the search and the people cheered. They praised the soldiers, applauding, as the remaining men and women of the lineup hesitantly lowered their arms.

The body was thrown in the truck with the condemned.

options.name: The radio told of patriots, heroes, who aided in the identification of traitors to Spain.

title: Fall of Bilbao
desc:
Mateo sat on the soft grass bank, disregarding the booms and cracks of weapons in the distance. Despite the darkness, the area was illuminated as though it were day.

He was a painter. Exposed in some local exhibitions, his skill was noted but he was by no means famous - something that had never dampened his spirit. He had purchased an apartment near the City's fine art museum for that reason, a regular reminder of his most cherished wish - for his paintings to be as well regarded as the art inside that fine building. Before, he had often gone there, seeing the classics. He had watched the nearby river and its traffic, the people who had once filled the area. All now absent.

Now he sat before the museum as it burned, an inferno illuminating all around it like a second sun. Carlos felt flat, his emotion seemingly having run dry. He watched the fire, the smoke that disappeared into the night sky silhouetted against the stars. A stray shell? Deliberate arson? Were those classics he had once looked upon so lovingly inside the furious orange rage before him? He didn't know.

On the ground was a canvas, beside him paints and brush. As he had seen the building as he had stumbled through the streets, the fire then in its infancy but building fast, dark inspiration had struck. He had raced home, disregarding the dangers, fetching these art supplies. They were his last, maybe the last in the entire city now, but they would serve to capture the final moments of one of the few monuments to civilization that remained in the city.

Without a twitch he captured the titanic fire and its tremendous heat, the glimpses of the proud building that had once stood there. Mateo felt no emotion, his face creased in concentration rather than grief, but the painting expressed it all. A final ironic ode to beauty against the backdrop of savagery.

options.name: One last masterpiece amongst the devastation.

title: Fall of Cadiz
desc:
The two families huddled around the fire they had built with faces blacked by grime, their clothes no more than rags. They were in a garage, connected to a large apartment bloc that had been built before the war. The fire burned in an old garbage can. A cruel act of fate meant the nights were the coldest seen in a generation.

The leader of the Ramirez family, Josephina, spoke up first. She was with her surviving children - she did not know where her husband was. They stood still, staring at the fire silently. The youngest, a girl no older than 4, clung to a disfigured doll.

"We should go to the port, find a boat" Josephina said bluntly.

The leader of the Torrez family, the teenage José, simply looked at her blankly. His siblings shivered, their parents long since buried, the fire insufficient to ease their suffering. The clothes they all wore were huge, stuffed with plastic bags to try and provide some warmth from the cold night air.

Josephina placed her hands as close to the scant fire as she could, refusing to look at the Torrezs. "We won't stay here. We could try and reach Portugal, or maybe Morocco is more peaceful..." She trailed off. She had no idea of where to go, or the situation anywhere outside Cadiz.

"I won't stop you" José said blankly. "We are staying though. We can't run anymore. We've dug too many graves."
