Our sources in the Portuguese Confederation have informed us that they do not expect the new government to attempt any provocation, not to mention an outright attack, on the Spanish at any point in the foreseeable future - very few in Portugal wish to return to the days of the Union, and even if they did, the government will have to spend years rebuilding Portugal's devastated infrastructure and shattered institutions before they could even think about invading the much larger Spain.

That being the case, it seems that this issue has been mostly resolved. Some in our sources consider it likely that the Spanish will attempt some sort of provocation on the Portuguese border at some point - but the Spanish are just as battered as the Portuguese, and it seems that Iberia should be able to know a few years of peace at the very least.

options.name: On to the next issue!

title: The Spanish Insist on Portuguese Military Restrictions
desc:
Despite our numerous attempts to placate the Spanish, telling them that the Portuguese government would not have the will or the capacity to attempt any serious provocation, let alone an invasion, as well as offering them our guarantee to hold back the Portuguese even in the off chance that they get the idea of crossing the border, the Spanish have refused to budge. They have informed us in no uncertain terms that they will not acquiesce to any restoration of the Portuguese state that does not provide them with robust means of enforcing strict military restrictions on it.

Our negotiators are quite dismayed by this development. While not our preferred contestant to come out of the wreckage of the union, many in the State Department had hoped the regime could be reasonable - apparently, this is not the case. We do, however, still have a few possible choices to make.

Some delegates propose simply acquiescing to the Spanish demands - unsatisfying as it may be, it will help smooth things over with the regime and enable us to work with them in the future, pragmatically if not cordially. Others suggest we agree to the Spanish demands in principle, but demand that a more impartial third party oversee the maintenance of the military restrictions, hopefully without undermining the viability of the Portuguese state. However, a growing clique of State Department officials are now openly calling for us to walk out of the negotiations - if the Spanish believe that they can force us to bend to their every whim, they will have to learn their lesson the hard way.

options.name: This is the Spaniards' backyard, after all...
We understand their legitimate concerns, but an impartial observer will have to do.
This farce has gone on long enough.

title: The Americans Offer Third Party Oversight of Military Restrictions
desc:
After forwarding our demands of restrictions on the new Portuguese armed forces and of Spanish oversight of their implementation, the American delegation has come back with a suggestion of their own.

The Americans have agreed in principle to the idea of restricting the Portuguese military to avoid any future bloodshed on the peninsula. However, they claim that Spanish oversight of these restrictions would be itself unconducive to the stability of the future Portuguese state, and cite concerns for its sovereignty. Instead, they propose that a third party, trusted by both sides, be tasked with overseeing the implementation of these restrictions. This way, the Americans claim, peace on the peninsula could be maintained without undermining the viability of the Portuguese state.

For some in our delegation, this is more than acceptable - it would free up resources we could use to stabilise our own war-torn nation, and as long as the third party is trustworthy enough, there should be no cause for concern. Others, however, claim that only we have an interest to ensure the restrictions are properly upheld, and that any third party, no matter how well-intentioned, may well allow a revanchist Portuguese regime to fester under its nose - until it will explode in their faces, and in ours.

options.name: A neutral observer would suffice.
This American protectorate was never going to be sovereign anyways...

title: The Spanish Reject Third Party Oversight Over Portugal
desc:
After offering to accept the Spanish demands for oversight over the implementation of Portuguese military restriction, but on the condition that said oversight will be undertaken by a neutral third party, there was cautious optimism in our delegation. It was hoped that the Spanish would see sense and let the Portuguese rebuild without undue interference in their affairs.

Those hopes have now been dashed. In a memorandum, the Spanish delegates have informed us that Madrid considers any Portuguese government not overseen by them as a grave security risk - too grave to accept. They will have the right of supervision over the Portuguese armed forces, or there will be no agreement.

Our diplomats are furious - Portugal will be too weak to attempt any provocation against the Spanish even if they had wanted to, and the Spanish demand to have direct oversight over their armed forces is a barefaced power grab. Many of them claim that the Spanish have made clear they will not be negotiating in good faith, and that there is no reason for negotiations to continue. Others claim that, even if the Spanish have shown themselves to be untrustworthy, there is still much we can gain from these negotiations - the potential of a gateway into Europe may be too enticing to pass up...

options.name: This is pointless.
Do we really care about Portugal, anyway?

title: The Spanish Ask for Reparations
desc:
The negotiations with the Spanish have been tense at times, but they have held so far. While we are almost ready to declare negotiations a success, the Spanish delegation have come forward with a final request: they demand that Portugal pays reparations to Spain - as the successors of the Iberian Union, the Spanish claim that the Portuguese secession has affected them adversely and that it is within their right to request a remedial payment.

The patience of many of our delegates with the Spanish diplomats was already running thin, and now many are calling for us to walk out of these negotiations entirely - the Spanish are plainly trying for a cash grab and have proven time and again that they are not acting in good faith. These delegates demand that we now confront the Spanish about their unscrupulous behavior - we can't let them extort us endlessly.

While almost none in our delegation believe that levying this payment from the Portuguese would be desirable, even if it was possible, some claim that we can spare the money for the Spanish demands, and that this is, all things considered, not a deal breaker. They suggest that we offer the Spanish the money they desire, but through an alternative source - for a relatively small sum, we could arrive at an advantageous result in these negotiations.

options.name: Let's sweeten the pot a little.
Time to draw a line in the sand.

title: The Americans Confront Us About Reperations
desc:
The Americans have refused our requested reparations, saying that it is not only impossible to obtain that amount from Portugal, but also the damages of the war are not nearly equivalent to our requested sum. We had hoped to secure enough funding to bounce back our economy, but that is looking more and more tenuous. Many of our delegation still hold strong to the demands though, and are looking into alternatives that, while not what we may deserve from the Portuguese, could be what we need.

Others suggest walking out on the brazen Americans who are demanding so much while giving so little. They stand strong on Portuguese accountability for the civil war, though perhaps scrapping the reparations and demanding an apology and national accountability would appease them, and our people. Blame falls on them for letting the situation in Iberia spiral so disastrously out of control, and we refuse to let our national pride be damaged without any sort of redress.

It's that, or we walk out.

options.name: How dare they! Leave them at the table.
Our economy can deal without the money, but our people need an apology.
Propose an alternative for reparations. 'Route' the money through the OFN.

title: The Spanish Demand An Apology
desc:
Some of the more sensible heads of the Spanish delegation have come forward and acknowledged our points on the Portuguese reparations, but they still have to appease some of their more nationalistic colleagues and have a proposal for us.

Though the Confederation had no participation in the war itself, it will be the successor state to Portugal and thus the Spanish are demanding the nation take accountability for the civil war and publicly apologize for the devastation it has caused. The Spanish say that this is enough for them, and it may even give the Confederation's government some legitimacy, in a backwards sort of way.

Our delegation doesn't love it, and the Portuguese even less, but we aren't gonna get a better deal. After this, we can call it closed and move to the next steps. All in all, it's worth the headache.

options.name: If it'll make you happy.

title: The Spanish Propose An Alternative
desc:
Our protests at the reparations have borne some fruit, the Spanish are willing to make a compromise. They need money, and they need the Portuguese to take accountability for the war, but the money doesn't have to come from the Portuguese. Publicly, if we route the reparations through the OFN, we can foot the bill and put Portugal back in Iberia. It's not the best deal, but we had already considered the option in the past and it's a small price to pay to have an OFN foothold on the continent.

The Confederation are willing to publicly take accountability, though they certainly aren't happy about it. Knowing they won't collapse paying reparations though, has mollified them to the idea a bit. If we do this we can be done with negotiations and look towards the next steps, whatever those may be.

This way everyone is happy and Uncle Sam pays the tab.

options.name: What else is new, where do we sign.
That's not a burden we can bear right now.

title: American Delegation Shuts Down The Bid
desc:
Perhaps it was too obvious of Madrid's intent to ride the tiger on the negotiations, as the United States' response to the Spanish demands were anything but conciliatory; It is abundantly clear that Portuguese reparations are out of the question, with the Americans clearly growing impatient with their Spanish counterparts.

The American response was by no means unforeseen; They could clearly see the attempt to milk the situation to our betterment, evidently no pushover in shrewd brinkmanship in their own right. If nothing else, we have reaffirmed our capacity for cunning diplomacy on the world stage and shown slough in this regard either.

There is still something to be gained from this however; Even if reparations are out of our reach, we can still demand a formal apology from the Portuguese for refusing to reintegrate with Spanish leadership, thus sparking the recent conflict between Madrid and Lisbon. It would be a decent manner of which to save diplomatic face over the loss of reparations, yet some will argue that this is simply too petty on the part of the Spanish and that dropping the issue would be preferable to alienating ourselves further in the negotiations.

options.name: We can't leave Azores/Madeira without a Portuguese admission of culpability, demand an apology.
This is vindictive even for us, just let the matter drop.

title: The United States Offers A Solution
desc:
Never known for a straightforward remedy for foreign entanglements, the Washington delegation in the Azores/Madeira has presented a resolution regarding reparations for Spain. Not wanting to levy the delivery of reparations onto the Portuguese, the Americans are instead pushing for said reparations to be 'routed' through the OFN, providing Spain the desired concessions in a manner that keeps the weight of financing them off of Portugal's shoulders.

One can argue we gained more than we ought to given the circumstances; Demanding reparations was an obvious ploy, one that the Americans may be well aware of in their decision making. The United States might have an earnest interest in keeping the economic costs out of Portugal's pocket, still in recovery after the multiplicative wars following the Iberian Collapse, thus prompting the decision to use OFN channels to fulfill the Spanish demands.

The exact logistics of this are not yet set in stone however, in so much that it might be by design; It's possible that utilizing OFN channels would tie it up in OFN bureaucracy as a means to stall or stymie the reparations through a mountain of red tape. Besides, it was Portuguese obstinacy that propagated the Spanish invasion and reparations should naturally fall on their head. We could play the safe route and take the American offer as it stands, but it might be prudent to demand Portugal themselves pay if this turns out to be yet another OFN ruse.

options.name: The Yanqui connives, the Spainard reaps the benefit; Let the OFN pay reparations
We can never know how deep the OFN rabbit hole goes; Demand Portugal pay reparations.

title: Portugal shuts down OFN reparations, demands that Portugal must pay.
desc:
Spanish shicannery in foreign policy is seemingly never not in style, as shown in the recent demands of Madrid. Despite the offer to pay reparations out of the OFN's own pocket, Spain is insistent that the Portuguese should be made to pay. Despite their insistence that Portugal is at fault for causing the war, one can assume that there are more pedestrian reasons for their demands; A combination of a financial injection combined with a desire to humiliate Portugal, maybe even as a means to depress their economy as to force them to be more reliant on Spain's.

It is perhaps still possible that the Spanish will see reason in allowing the OFN to compensate Madrid in some other way down the line; They know as well as we do they can only push this issue so far and may still bite if an offer is on the table. Then again, most wars are bound to leave scars and Spain's invasion of Portugal is only the latest chapter of violence after the Iberian collapse. They might not be willing to take no for an answer in forcing Portugal to pay.

If worse comes to worse, we can have Portugal agree to paying reparations, however appalling that might be. There are humanitarian interests within the OFN concerned with providing foreign aid on the ground to the people of Portugal, something that would hopefully take some of the sting out of the cost of meeting the Spanish demands. We need to attempt to keep Spain on a cordial basis with the west and as much as the OFN can, we should at least try to minimize the suffering in Portugal while placating the Spanish at the same time.

options.name: Does it really matter where the money comes from? Offer OFN compensation.
It is the OFN owes Portugal a great debt after this, whatever Madrid thinks; Have Portugal pay.

title: The Failure of the Azores Negotiations
desc:
The conference room was as sterile as a blank canvas, stark against the muted, faded majesty of what was otherwise bespoke, old European stylings of the building that housed it. A gray-maned party official of the National Front stood before a cramped cluster of microphones erected together on a podium. A line of journalists and media representatives from news agencies the world over sat bunched together as if attending chapel.

By late afternoon that day, many would consider doing just that; Some did, others did not.

As part of a direct correspondence from Madrid to the Spanish people, the party official announced that Spain had formally withdrawn from the negotiations in the Azores/Madeira. Placing the blame for the negotiations' failure squarely at the feet of the United States of America, whose rank, imperious greed sought to usurp Portuguese autonomy in the name of capital.

Without outwardly addressing the current state of affairs regarding the Portuguese Confederation in the south Atlantic or their allies in the OFN, the party official announced that Spanish National Forces would at last be withdrawing from Portugal effective immediately, with the government in Madrid working to establish to a new government in Lisbon.

A chorus of concern followed the party official out of the room as the conference concluded, declining further inquiries where it related to the Portuguese for the time being; "Will there be war with the United States?" "Would the Azores/Madeira remain independent?" "What of the Germans or the Italians' involvement?" None of these questions would be answered right away, they simply hung in the air.

As the news representatives were quietly ushered out, a single crack in the high ceiling sent a tiny piece of decades-old plaster tumbling onto the shoulder of a young journalist making for the front door. It would be brushed off with barely a second thought, only to be vaguely remembered later. But briefly, a strange symmetry could be seen, even if not by any of the men and women there at that moment.

options.name: Some institutions are not made to move simply because it is demanded of them, some blemishes must be tolerated until the new paint dries.

title: The Failure of the Azores Negotiations
desc:
To the Office of the President of the United States of America; After Action Report: The Azore Negotiations.

Mr. President.

As was indicated as a potentiality in previous correspondence as is the case at present, the delegation representing the Spanish government have announced their formal withdrawal from the Azores Negotiations. Despite the US' best attempts at placating Spanish demands while safeguarding OFN interests in Portugal, Madrid has proven an obstacle to any perceived encroachment within their sphere of influence.

As of yesterday, Spanish military forces have withdrawn from Occupied Portugal, beginning the process of establishing a provisional government with Spanish supervision. The Portuguese interior is still under reconstruction after the invasion, with low domestic support for the provisional government or their allies in Madrid.

So far, no inroads have been made regarding the OFN backed administration in the Azores/Madeira have been made by the Spanish leadership, but we have little reason to believe that relations will remain cordial for long so long as a rival Portuguese government in the south Atlantic continues to exist.

We advise the Office of the Presidency to consider every option at its' disposal; Joint US/OFN forces in the south Atlantic remain on standby, as do the necessary naval assets to support the Portuguese Confederation in a land invasion of mainland Portugal should conflict break out with Spanish-aligned government in Lisbon.

We are certain that whatever course of action you commit to will be the correct one in preserving the interests of both the United States of America and her OFN commitments.

Yours sincerely,
The United States Department of State.

options.name: People have argued for years that putting up with Franco was a bad idea, maybe time is finally proving them right.

title: Portugal Returns!
desc:
The press conference was like so many others had been in the past. Loud, bombastic, full of smug-looking bureaucrats - and inescapable, on every channel of note. As the citizens of the State watched it over dinner, the announcements were made clear.

An agreement had been reached between Spain and Portugal, as represented by the Americans. Spain was to withdraw from Portuguese territory, and allow the Confederation to return and assume sovereignty over Portugal itself. Instructions had already been issued to the ministries and to military command, and it was expected that the withdrawal would begin shortly.

The spokesman was clear that Spain was to benefit from this agreement, economically and otherwise. Some more astute viewers, however, quickly noticed that despite his attestation that concessions were reasonable and minor in comparison to the gains made, he was careful not to detail them.

That would no doubt come in time. Those watching were torn. Many welcomed back their former Iberian brothers and sisters to the peninsula, others were cautiously optimistic over the 'benefits' that were supposedly to come. Others wondered what had been conceded. But all agreed that Spain, even under the Union, never did anything without a goal in mind.

options.name: The State has achieved its goals.

title: Successful Summit with Spain!
desc:
The State Department has reported that the negotiations with Spain over the status of the Portuguese Confederation and its territory in Iberia proper have been successful.

The Spanish have agreed to allow the Confederation to return and assume full political control over Portuguese territory. It is expected that their military and civilian assets will begin the process of withdrawal imminently. This should be seen for the significant win that it is, demonstrating the commitment of the OFN to peaceful resolution of national disputes.

This victory is not without cost, however. Concessions were made in order to acquire Spanish agreement, and these will need to be paid in full. Beyond that, Portugal as a whole is still badly damaged from the conflict, and enormous investment will be needed in order to allow for proper reconstruction - investment that the Confederation will surely consider its due.

Of course, however, there is opportunity even in that. Reconstruction will have to be performed by companies capable of doing so, of course. And America has so many of those that would be more than pleased to assist.

options.name: A victory for the free world.

title: Return of the Exiles
desc:
FROM: Ministry of Foreign Affairs
TO: The Council of Ministers
SUBJECT: The Return of the Portuguese Confederation

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has received a request from the American Department of State to negotiate the potential return of the OFN-aligned Portuguese Confederation to Spanish-occupied lands in Portugal.

- The islands are under the control of the illegitimate Portuguese Confederation after their failure to seize control of Portugal during the Portuguese Civil War.
- The Portuguese Confederation is a pro-OFN organization, with lobbies in OFN member states such as Brazil. Should the Confederation ever take power in Lisbon, it will turn Portugal into an important foothold for the OFN in Europe.
- We will require concessions from the OFN in order to allow the return of the Portuguese Confederation to Lisbon.
- Should we fail to negotiate with the OFN, they may prefer to deal with the Confederation without us. From the islands, the Confederation may be able to launch an invasion of Portugal if sufficiently trained and equipped.

We recommend engagement with the Americans on this issue.

options.name: Agreed. Let's see where this gets us.
Declined. We don't want to negotiate.

title: Return of the Exiles
desc:
FROM: Ministry of Foreign Affairs
TO: The Council of Ministers
SUBJECT: The Return of the Portuguese Confederation

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has received a message from the American Department of State regarding the return of the OFN-aligned Portuguese Confederation to Lisbon.

- The Portuguese Confederation had been exiled to the archipelagos of Azores and Madeira after their failure to seize control of Portugal during the Portuguese Civil War.
- The Portuguese Confederation is a pro-OFN organization, with lobbies in OFN member states such as Brazil.
- A longstanding objective of the Portuguese Confederation was to return to Portugal and establish Republican rule in Lisbon.
- Due to friendly relations with the OFN and Portuguese Confederation, we have voluntarily returned our occupied Portuguese lands to the Portuguese Confederation.
- All exiles in the Portuguese Confederation are pardoned and welcome to return to Iberia safely without fear of repression.

The State Department and Portuguese Ministry of Foreign Affairs express their deepest gratitude to the Iberian Council of Ministers.

options.name: Welcome home at last.

title: Operation Sebastian Completes Preparations
desc:
FROM: US State Department
TO: President [USA.GetLeader]
SUBJECT: Portuguese Confederation completes Invasion Preperations.

The Portuguese Confederation, the remnants of the Portuguese Republic that were able to evacuate to the Atlantic Archipelagos, have completed their preparations to retake the mainland. Operation Sebastian, as the invasion is codenamed, shall commence imminently unless we intervene.

- Direct costs to the US are minimal as, while sponsored by the US, most committed forced source from the Portuguese themselves.
- In the event of success, the Confederation would represent guarantee a pro-OFN Portugal, granting us a strategically significant nation within Europe.
- In the event of failure, the US would lose very little directly beyond some material, and would be in a position to obtain new administrations within the Atlantic Archipelagos. Since a failed invasion would almost certainly collapse Confederation authority and legitimacy on the Islands, the United States would be best poised to serve as the islands' new guarantors.
- It would be possible to use the Confederation's reliance upon us for their authority to pressure them to cease invasion preparations. Such an action would almost certainly lead to a collapse of the Government, however it would allow the UNited States to establish its authority over the islands with a much higher degree of smoothness compared to a failed invasion.
State Department proposals on the structure of an Azores and Madeira stabilisation mission shall be provided in the coming days.

options.name: The Confederation has our support and our faith. Godspeed.
An invasion with few prospects threatens our position in the Atlantic. Pressure against invasion.

title: Operation Sebastian Begins
desc: RPP will invade the Portugal winner. This event doesn't need loc now because you aren't meant to play as RPP at this stage in the current build.

options.name: Let's go

title: Operation Sebastian Completes Preparations
desc:
FROM: US State Department
TO: President [USA.GetLeader]
SUBJECT: Portuguese Confederation completes Invasion Preperations.

The Portuguese Confederation, the remnants of the Portuguese Republic that were able to evacuate to the Atlantic Archipelagos, have completed their preparations to retake the mainland. Operation Sebastian, as the invasion is codenamed, shall commence imminently unless we intervene. A potentially significant development is the current mainland administration is being invaded by Spain.

- Direct costs to the US are minimal as, while sponsored by the US, most committed forced source from the Portuguese themselves.
- In the event of success, the Confederation would represent guarantee a pro-OFN Portugal, granting us a strategically significant nation within Europe.
- In the event of failure, the US would lose very little directly beyond some material, and would be in a position to obtain new administrations within the Atlantic Archipelagos. Since a failed invasion would almost certainly collapse Confederation authority and legitimacy on the Islands, the United States would be best poised to serve as the islands' new guarantors.
- It would be possible to use the Confederation's reliance upon us for their authority to pressure them to cease invasion preparations. Such an action would almost certainly lead to a collapse of the Government, however it would allow the UNited States to establish its authority over the islands with a much higher degree of smoothness compared to a failed invasion.
- The current invasion of Portugal from Spain makes an invasion far more likely to succeed, however it also opens questions about what would occur in the event of a Spanish victory before the Confederation could fully establish itself. We can also pressure the Confederation to postpone the invasion until the resolution of the mainland conflict, to consider if the outcome may be to our mutual benefit.

options.name: The Confederation has our support and our faith. Godspeed.
A risky invasion threatens our position in the Atlantic. Pressure against invasion.
Peninsula developments may give us Portugal without firing a shot. Postpone and watch for now.

title: El Amigo Americano
desc:
In a small room in the guts of the Pearl of Andalusia’s town hall, two men conversed. One spoke in his native language, the other in a language acquired and honed by training. Pío Cabanillas placed one hand on the arm of his chair and began, "Señor Fig, you must understand the situation. Our forces are bolstered with the people’s will, but they need arms. Our manufactories cannot yet provide for us by themselves. We need aid from the United States, and we need it soon."

Agent Frances "Fig" Coleman sat back in his chair, adjusting his square glasses slightly. "It’s already on the way. The State Department approved the first shipment yesterday, and assuming it has no trouble crossing the Atlantic, you’ll see it by the end of the week. The problem-" The Pennsylvania native leaned forward, his face coming into the light. "-is with members of your government. State is concerned that the more left-leaning parts of your opposition and the return of the huidos and maquisards may pose a threat to a freedom-allied Spain in the aftermath of your victory. I remember the Lincoln Battalion, and Washington does too, but we can’t brook any chances that our two nations’ relationship might go into jeopardy."

Pío gave Fig a half-smile, and then said, "Get me the guns, mines, and rockets, and I can be remarkably unstinting in my praise of the OFN."

At that, Fig gave his own half-smile, extended a hand, and said, "Then you have my answer."

options.name: Building a friendship on spent casings.

title: The Prodigal Return
desc:
José Gómez Gordoa had never liked the so-called 'Mexican' Pavilion in Sevilla. But his likes mattered little, given that it had been officially designated as the temporary embassy for Mexico and he, as the Chargé d’Affaires, was obligated to use it. Mayan stylings and all.

Standing between two carved Toltec-styled serpent heads, he addressed a small audience of officials and prominent figures from the Sevillan government. Mexico City had been clear with him, and he was now clear with them, that Mexico considered the government here in Sevilla as the official successor of both the exiled republic and of Spanish democracy in general. He spoke strongly of Mexico, and how it, of course, had deep ties to Spain - and would step up to protect one of its progenitors.

This entailed direct support, along with anything else that could be provided. Mexico, he announced, stood ready to do anything in its power to expel the fascists - and any other form of fascism - from Spain once and for all. Spain had crossed the ocean once, changing Mexico forever. Mexico would now do the same, crossing in reverse to change Spain.

As he finished speaking, he took a step back to claps and cheers. Gordoa felt deep satisfaction, and he looked forward to mediating between Sevilla and Mexico City. He only wished that a better building could be found soon.

options.name: The statues looked on.

title: Washington Extends a Hand
desc:
Ridgway B Knight, American Chargé d’Affaires to the newly-proclaimed Spanish Republic, shook hands with President Humberto Delgado before the acting President beckoned him to take a seat on a nearby couch. Knight had only recently arrived in Spain, and so his schedule and staff were in a chaotic state at the moment, although it seemed like the Republic was under similar circumstances. After some initial pleasantries, Knight leapt straight into the heart of their meeting today, "President Delgado, I can assure you Washington is very interested in deepening relations with the Republic. They've agreed to send military and economic aid to help the Republic defeat the Kingdom and reunify Spain under a democratic government."

Delgado's face, already lit up by the confirmation that aid would be on its way, brightened even further after Knight passed him a folder containing what equipment would be arriving in the first shipments from across the pond. "Thank you, thank you, we won't forget this generosity. With America on our side, all of Spain may soon be liberated from the grip of fascism."

Delgado paused for a moment, and then spoke, "About the Atlantic archipelagos," Knight's jaw tightened a bit, "is there any chance of Washington aiding in an operation to reclaim them? It's a daunting task for us alone considering the circumstances."

Knight knew that Madeira and the Azores were currently under the control of Admiral Fernando, and that the OFN wasn't eager to burn that bridge just yet. Knight stood up and made his way towards the door as he gave his response, "I'm sorry, I can't comment on that just yet, and I unfortunately am needed elsewhere for another meeting with my staff." He was out the door before President Delgado had a chance to probe further.

options.name: And just like that, the meeting was concluded.

title: To Hold The Whip-Hand
desc:
The gentle patter of rain upon the roof graced Lisboa as the ship pulled into port. Among her passengers was Aguinaldo Boulitreau Fragoso, a Brazilian diplomat, and receiving him in Belém Palace was Acting President Humberto Delgado.

A warm smile was exchanged, and the diplomat’s guard stood outside the room the two men sat down in. Delgado began, saying, "Let me first tell you how honored I am that the men of your republic have lent diplomatic support to mine. I have always said the lusophone nations must stick together, and just hosting you here has increased my standing in parliament."

Fragoso smiled at his flattery. "Of course, Presidente. Brazil will always be steadfast in its contributions to liberty, and that, of course, extends to our mother country. There is strong support for you and your republic in Brasília. The dockworkers are putting shipments of aid together around the clock–Jesucristo knows we want to help."

Fragoso leaned back in his chair and then continued, "You’ll be pleased to know that your mainland exiles have also begun sending donations along with the aid. They’re relatively modest in wealth, but their thoughts and hopes are with you for a free Portugal."

Delgado grinned humbly. "I know we will not let them down. Thank you for your aid, and your time. If I'm ever in Recife, I trust I can look you up?" Fragoso gave an enigmatic look.

options.name: "No doubt, Senhor. No doubt."

title: A Second Offer for a Second Civil War
desc:
Tomás García Rebull, shook hands with Hans Hoffmann, someone Rebull was already familiar with considering the German diplomat's long career in both Spain and Iberia. Rebull was careful not to show that he was nervous, since this meeting could very well decide how the next few years for all of Spain would play out, let alone the fate of the National Junta itself. After greetings and sitting down, Hoffmann handed Rebull a dossier, "That is a list of all the equipment and aid Germania is willing to send over at this time," said Hoffmann.

Rebull flipped through the dossier, the vice-president could hardly believe his eyes as the list just kept on going and going. Rifles, economic aid, food, trucks, explosives, artillery, planes, and even tanks were all printed out on the dossier. It was such good news Rebull knew there had to be a catch. "This is quite a lot of aid. Not that we aren't grateful, but may I ask what the price tag will be for all of this? I am quite aware of the debt Spain had with Germany when you helped in the last civil war."

Hoffmann gave a slight chuckle and waved his hand, "There's no need to worry about that. We're not in 1936 anymore, circumstances have changed. Now it is Germania's perspective that securing your government's survival is a matter of continental security, and one of utmost importance."

Rebull eyed the German diplomat's expression during his response, trying to tell if the man was trying to pull the wool over his eyes. However, Hoffmann's face did not betray him, and Rebull simply could not get a read on the man. While he couldn't fully trust it, Rebull wasn't about to look a gift horse in the mouth, "Well then, we thank you again for the generosity, and you can inform your superiors they can begin the shipments as soon as possible."

options.name: And so the deal was signed.

title: A Meeting With Rome
desc:
José María Codón welcomed Francesco Cavalletti di Oliveto Sabino, the Italian Chargé d’Affaires, into his office. As foreign minister of the national Junta, it was not the most grandiose of meeting places, but the chairs were comfortable and the view outside the windows was pleasant enough for its purpose. Sabino was quick to get to business, cutting through the initial pleasantries, "I can speak on behalf of Rome when I say that the Kingdom of Italy is willing to send aid to your government in its bid to reunify Spain."

Codón was sure he was smiling as he responded, "That's great news! We assure you that we will use any aid to the best of-"

"However, that aid shall only arrive on one condition: That your government keeps its distance from Germany and instead stays closer to Italy."

Codón couldn't say the condition was unexpected, but it was going to make things much more complicated. After trying to formulate a satisfying response, he spoke, "While I personally prefer Rome over Germania, I am but one man. I can try to express the importance of fulfilling your condition to the rest of the Junta's leadership, but I can't move mountains by myself. If you want to see us move towards Italy, your aid will need to be substantial."

options.name: Now it was Sabino's turn to say: "I'll see what I can do."

title: The Pakt's Oculus
desc:
The evening was hardly welcoming in Porto, with the sun having fallen well past the horizon. Without the street-lamps turned on, it was a sea of darkness.

In an administrative building on the Rua de Santa Catarina, João Pinto da Costa Leite, the Foreign Affairs man in the Kingdom of Portugal, was sitting behind a broad oak desk. Before him was Herbert Müller-Roschach, the newly-appointed charge d'affaires for the Kingdom. Costa Leite began in a mild, but strained tone, "I'm sure I don't need to tell you that our Kingdom needs friends. We are alone, and the Americans' puppets in Lisbon are baying for our blood."

Roschach returned that infuriatingly impassive look that it seemed all of the Reich's functionaries had mastered. "I am afraid you have been misled as to the nature of this mission. It is an observational one, not one to determine how much money and guns we funnel to you."

Costa Leite narrowed his eyes, and Roschach rolled his shoulders. "But...I was not sent here to play babysitter. If the Reich weren't interested in helping, I would not have been sent over in such haste." Roschach pressed his fingers together into a diamond. "Soon, I will send my report to Germania. On my own initiative, and with approval from the Abwehr station-chief, I will recommend aid be delivered, and your guns and money will come."

The lusophone's eyes cooled, and returned to their natural quality. "I...appreciate that, Senhor. Portugal's future foreign policy will surely be decided by your aid.

options.name: Eyes opened. Doors to follow.

title: Promises Yet Unfulfilled
desc:
Although the state dinner was well-attended by various government ministers, all attention was upon the foreign ambassadors present. There were not many, but each was seen as priceless, and each had to be correctly handled.

Earlier that day, they had, one by one, presented their credentials to Prime Minister Tavares and had them formally accepted. The Kingdom of Portugal desperately needed legitimacy and support both, and Tavares was working tirelessly to acquire them. Of all the ambassadors, however, his focus was upon Giuseppi Cerulli Irelli, the new representative of Italy to the resurgent Kingdom. The days of the Triumvirate were not forgotten, nor was the power of Italy relative to the other states.

As such, Tavares spoke warmly and often to Irelli during every course, looking for his opportunity - which came shortly after dessert and was, to his great surprise, advanced by Irelli himself. Safely ensconced away from the other ambassadors and their sensitive ears, Irelli communicated to Tavares that Rome was very interested in ensuring the Kingdom's success. That was very well and good, of course, but to Tavares' cautious delight, Irelli informed him that Italy was preparing to send over aid. Unconditionally - at least on the surface.

Tavares was warm and excessive in his genuine thanks. He did hedge, however, by stating his hopes that the 'aid' promised would be something other than scraps. Portugal needed more.

options.name: Irelli's tight smile did not give clarification.

title: The Pakt's Hands
desc:
The mid-morning sun had given way to a heavy rain beating down upon Porto's streets and citizens. Out of the rain and away from winds, another meeting was happening in the commercial district. Sheltered in a small, emptied cafe were the strange pair, Müller-Roschach and Costa Leite. Roschach sipped from his cold cup and looked at the Portuguese man with a grave face. "The coup was nasty business. It didn't come at such a good time, either. My friends in the Abwehr are no fools; they know Kaulza isn't interested in integration into the Reich's European order. I'm sure you know how tenuous support is right now. Germania is still interested in providing aid, but we might be pressed to reconsider if it will just end up in the hands of a hostile state instead of a strategic partner."

Costa Leite swallowed, understanding the gravity of the moment well. "Kaulza is...difficult. But even he needs allies. Trust me when I say you are still our Kingdom's best option."

He turned his eyes away, pondering the next words briefly."I can ensure Kaulza sets aside his differences with you in exchange for guns. He knows, or will know, that he can't survive without help. Keep the aid flowing, and I will make Kaulza understand the importance of our partnership with Germany."

Roschach nodded, although in the recesses of his mind, he began to feel a creeping emotion: doubt. Would the Kingdom of Portugal really prove to be the correct investment at the right time, or another farce? Well, he supposed, either way, the rifles will come to Iberia. They may as well be German.

options.name: Your right fist, O Lord, is majestic in power; Your right fist, O Lord, shattered the enemy.

title: An Unimportant Change
desc:
Looking out of his window, Giuseppe Cerulli Irelli surveyed what portions of Portugal he could see through the Italian embassy's gates. Gates that he had ordered closed for the time being out of polite caution.

The recent coup in the Kingdom had been very concerning, both to him and to Italy (though he considered those to be one and the same). The relationships he had formed with the government had been thrown into tumult, but upon careful examination and after receiving overtures, he was confident he had properly re-evaluated the landscape. Turning to his desk, he prepared his official missive to Rome.

Kaulza, now prime minister, was of course a radical of the highest order, as were the many officers he had brought forward and installed into high government positions. That was concerning, but the reality remained that Italy was a powerful and desirable ally, and Kaulza had made it clear that he would collaborate with anyone who could assist the Kingdom in achieving victory.

Of course, whoever did so would reap the value of influence and obligation, and Cerulli intended that Italy should be the beneficiary. He summarized that Rome should continue aid and, if possible, even increase it.

options.name: As long as Kaulza remembers his 'friends.'

title: A Peninsular Luncheon
desc:
Although Hans Hoffman was not nearly as content as he could have been, he certainly couldn't fault the luncheon that Ximénez de Sandoval, the National Council's foreign minister, had invited him to.

He knew the reason, of course. The Junta had collapsed, and all eyes were on the Reich. On whom it would support, and how strongly. Hoffman himself had been a strong supporter of the Junta, seeing it as the faction most likely to bring the war to a speedy conclusion - and thus reduce the need for the Reich to spend more treasure on the peninsula. That was no longer a possibility, though the sandwiches were quite nice.

Hoffman did, however, concede that the end result was not unpleasant to the Reich. After all, with the Falange taking full charge of the situation, at least ideological alignment between the governments could be well-maintained. Sandoval, for his part, was wholly focused on whether there would be any changes in German aid owing to the 'change' in government and, after another dessert, Hoffman gave his reassurances.

The Reich could hardly let its fascist brothers down, could it? Especially when they had such excellent catering.

options.name: Relief.

title: Support Between Peninsulas
desc:
Although Ximénez de Sandoval did not have high hopes for his meeting with the Italian representative, Oliveto Sabino surprised him more than he had originally thought possible.

The Junta's collapse had, of course, forced all of the National Council's backers to re-evaluate their positions, and Sandoval, for his part, doggedly worked to find out what they were. In his own mind, however, he had anticipated the Italians to pull out and had largely written them off. The Junta had given them a palatable muddling of ideology to sell domestically, and he had thought the Falange a step too far.

But he had been wrong. Sabino had made it clear that, though deliberations had been intense, Rome had decided to continue its program of aid and support to the new Council. Sandoval was, of course, quick in his praise, but Sabino had stopped him. Rome hoped, he said, that this aid could show the Council that they need not just throw themselves into Germany's arms. The greater game was always in play.

Sandoval himself scrambled to answer as diplomatically as possible, but there Sabino stopped him as well. He simply hoped - as did Italy - that Sandoval's own early predictions would not become reality.

options.name: As long as the aid flows.

title: A Faithful Friend
desc:
Carazo Hernández perspired softly in the baking heat of the day. Rays from the sun scattered gently upon the foreign minister's back as he sat in the comfortable cafe chair, dots of moisture appearing on his face. He offhandedly wished he could bring the cool air of the Palace of Viana to the sunny day, as he watched birds flit from branch to branch far above him. He dabbed at the sweat on his forehead with a handkerchief, but looked up when he saw an approaching figure.

Oliveto Sabino smiled a bit on his approach, and then found his seat across from the Spaniard. Hernández began, in a light tone, "A pleasure, Señor Sabino. Let me start by telling you how grateful I am for your sustained support after the demise of the Junta. Italy's help is much appreciated–in these troubled times, generosity goes a long way." A waitress arrived at the table, dropping off a pair of cups filled with cortado. The two men accepted their drinks, and Hernández indulged, the silky taste of espresso and milk eternally pleasant as he had a sip. Sabino drummed his fingers for a moment on the glass table.

"To tell you the truth, I have always liked Carlism better than Falangism. The Falange, while...orderly, in its way, did not have the grace and daring of the Carlists. It's my hope that Italian rifles and Italian money can carry your Kingdom to victory over your foes in this war. After that, we can see to the creation of true friendship between our two nations."

Hernández smiled at the Italian, and then picked up his cup. "To friendship, Signore."

options.name: A clink, and then a chuckle.

title: Foreign Assistance From [?new_supporter_id.GetName]
desc:
FROM: Ministry of Foreign Affairs
TO: The Council of Ministers
SUBJECT: Foreign Assistance From [?new_supporter_id.GetName]

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has received a foreign aid package from the [?new_supporter_id.GetAdjective] delegation to assist our ongoing war effort. This aid is intended to bolster our capacity to wage war against our enemies and defend our lands from hostile powers in Iberia.

[?new_supporter_id.GetAdjective] support has taken the form of logistical assistance, material resources, and military advisors. A detailed, exhaustive list is attached to this document.

The full scope of aid coming from the government of [?new_supporter_id.GetName] may change in the future. However, its arrival shows who [?new_supporter_id.GetName] truly stands with in this conflict.

options.name: Extend our deepest gratitude.

title: The Oldest Alliance
desc:
The two longshoremen, good friends, had long worked together at the port outside Leixões, in northern Portugal. They had seen ships from all over the world, and often wagered (in a friendly fashion) between themselves on recognition of the ships in the distance. This time, however, they had both lost their bet.

For the ships - more than one - flew the British flag. They had seen it before, of course, but it had been rare indeed in the years before all the trouble. As they helped offload the cargoes they recognized the telltale characteristics of military equipment - standardized packages, uniform stencilling, and the like. But they were both more interested in eavesdropping on the conversations between the ship's officers and the port officials.

The longshoremen shared the port captain's surprise, as nobody at Leixões had heard anything about British military aid to the Kingdom (and they all knew, but politely didn't mention, the many troubles Britain had gone, and was going through, back at home). The British captain grimly agreed, telling the officials not to expect more, given the focus of his government at home, but that the equipment was intended as a formal token of support.

After all, he said with what even the longshoremen thought was an all-too-perfect example of British stoicism, Britain may be having troubles at the moment, but 'it has been through them before, and Britain always remembers its friends. And its obligations.' The port captain shook his hand warmly, and the longshoremen felt the warmth between the men. It was a feeling that had been shared by many compatriots in the two countries, for many centuries prior and, hopefully, hence.

options.name: Since 1386.
iberiawars.1000.a

title: Faces in the Wind
desc:
The day was bright and warm, the sea calm. Waves tapped the shore, and João felt his own stomach undulate as he sat and watched. He flipped open a newspaper, the bright white of the new print gleaming in the sunlight. His eyes glided over the front page: more news of the war in Spain. Some battle, a short excerpt from a Franco speech, a statement from the King. He read.

"The situation in Spain is most regrettable. We can only offer our prayers for the preservation of the Spanish people and for a quick resolution to this conflict."

João flipped the page. The statement ended; the articles about battles and Franco's speech continued. He laid the paper aside and looked out to the docks. He had worked there once, during their last war. Then, the Spaniards had come. They hung about the docks, the men, women, and children, begging. He had been told only the vagrants remained; the rest found work further inland. Whatever they were, the sight of those husks that rasped pleas for money to buy some bread, only to be knocked around by police with batons, made him sick.

He spared coins for them whenever he could. How glad he was when they went away! The guilt went with them, and he could content himself that when and where they returned, they returned to intact villages, families, farms, and homes; he could imagine no other.

João was not a sophisticated man; he did not know why they had fought then, nor did he know why now. Where he did not know. He stared into the horizon. He had heard that Portugal would not be spared this time, that already, the Republicans were mustering forces—that morning, he had read that his grandson would be enlisting in the King's forces. He picked up the paper and flipped to the sports section. The wind hurled, the waves crashed, and João huddled and read.

options.name: A storm approaches.

title: For Whom the Bell Tolls
desc:
The Lisbon morning began as so many others had, with the soft grazing of the Tagus, the distant ringing of the church bells, and menial shifting of papers in Delgado's office, as he quietly fanned documents around, testing to see if any caught his eye. His fingers paused as he swept over a headline, coated with an ink darker than the others:

CIVIL CONFLICT BREAKS OUT IN SPAIN

A deep toll sounded through the city.

1936. Delgado almost smiled at the title's symmetry from decades ago. What's next? Germany invading Poland, or whatever country they could get their decrepit hands on? He read further. The picture of the familiar tricolor, the Republican purple, gloriously unfurled against the sky.

A resonant toll sounded through the city.

Delgado picked up his pen, planting it on a sheet of paper before stopping. He could already imagine it. A letter to their leader. A pledge of unity for the Republican cause, from Lisbon to Madrid. He imagined walking onto the palace balconies to the roars of liberation. He imagined welcoming their leader to a stroll along the Tagus in Lisbon. He imagined victory.

A rhythmic toll sounded through the city.

Victory. A fragile word. When victory was possible in '36, '37, '38. History had a way to deceive those who believe in victory. Radiant like the light that spilled across the Tagus, but imperceptible to those blinded by only ideals. The Republicans — no, Spain — would not fall to such follies anymore. There were moments when a nation could feel itself at a precipice, at a new dawn. When the air rumbled with energy. Though the old Republicans were gone, men around Spain would allow themselves to believe in a new morning to end the Iberian nightmare.

options.name: The bell tolls for thee.

title: What Time Hath Wrought
desc:
Francisco Franco was a harsh thing to look at in his old age. In a room with his most esteemed members of both the government and military, he knew it was something more like a den of vipers. Unlike the Franco of the thirties, bold, disciplined, and every inch the revolutionary general, the Franco sitting slumped in the chair was the exhausted administrator. Years without daring had turned him torpid, and the stress of keeping together his nation under crisis made him look at least a decade older than he truly was. "Men of Spain, we must turn to the matter of... "

Across the room was Carlos Iniesta Cano. His eyes met the gaze of another man, wearing the same expression. For both men and many more, their faith in Franco, once ironclad, had withered away. Cano was one of those who had watched the Caudillo in his youth and saw as governance sanded off the edges of his true spirit. Spain, he believed, was rotting just like Franco. A great man had to take control, or the country that Cano and the old blueshirts loved so dearly would fall further. Cano looked into the crystal glass sitting to his right, its swirling waters and scant ice cubes, and then peered up at the clock. The meeting draggedEvery second Franco remained at the helm was a second Spain strayed nearer to further trials.

On the street, a clerk at the local FET office felt his blood boil as it tended to do often nowadays. He saw men in fatigues shouting orders as soldiers piled into APCs, speeding off to beat more Spaniards. His father, a soldier in the Mixed Brigades, had taught him all he needed to know about the bastards. Conmen who had stolen Spain's future in favor of jackboots on faces. Their ego had burned the Piel de Toro in '36, and soon it would burn the land again. It was nearly enough to make him weep, but before it could, an idea took hold in the young man's mind. Perhaps this was not the only way. Perhaps Spain could still be saved. Peace, progress... and elusive democracy. There were other men, his father's friends, who had fought in the War. Maybe it was time to reach out to them again.

options.name: The journey of a thousand miles...

title: History Rhymes
desc:
Urgent Dispatch
[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

Reichsminister,

The Spanish pretenders have formally surrendered to their rightful authority; our support has enabled the return of stability to this nation. President Cano informs me that our diplomatic staff shall return to Madrid soon. It is intended that the impending national victory parade to be held in the capital shall include a place of honor for ourselves; a large German contingent being arranged. He forwards an invitation to you, should you wish to attend the event.

The nation is decimated; many cities were subjected to mass destruction tactics and many areas of the countryside are lawless outside of core areas. I have, as instructed, offered our expertise in the stabilisation of such territories, and opened the possibilities of further financial and military cooperation with Germania. Once proposals are finalized by the Spanish, their requests shall be forwarded.

To avoid the distance developed between the Reich and Spain following their previous conflict, efforts are being taken to embed ourselves into the reconstruction process. The embassy is using the remains of war resources at our disposal to benefit officials identified as sympathetic to co-operation. We have encouraged references to racial fraternity and European cooperation in public messages from the embassy, to try and foster deeper ties between ourselves and Spain as many remain wary of the Reich's presence. Significantly, Foreign Minister Codón, remains hesitant towards Germania and continues to advocate for increased regional cooperation at the expense of the Reich - a view somewhat popular within the public. We must ensure every effort is taken to minimize this and bind them to us.

options.name: A victory rivaling 1939.

title: Corruption Unimpeded
desc:
Urgent Dispatch
[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

Reichsminister, 

The mouth of the Mediterranean has finally fallen, as the last chance for the victory of the final vestiges of rightful authority on the peninsula have surrendered themselves. All embassy staff, including myself, are being expelled, and I have been notified of a number of volunteers involved in our efforts to avert this outcome that are now interred by the new government. While the wider implications, especially in regards to foreign subversive influences, remain to be seen in Spain, in the short term it will be difficult to salvage anything from within the nation.

It is recommended that we maintain a continuity of operations in Germania. Many Spanish Falange have already, or are attempting, flight due to the hostility of the new administration. The creation of an organization for them to coordinate themselves and maintain our few remaining networks within the nation is essential if there is to be any hope of a reversal of our fortunes in the future. Further, pressure must be placed upon the new government to accept a diplomatic presence from the Reich and the rightful return of its citizens be they held by central or local authorities. We may have lost our preferential  access to the nation, but we must now seek to limit the malign influences within Spain that will seek to place themselves nearer to the Reich.Our one advantage is the devastation of the nation. Many cities lie in rubble and the countryside is devastated due to the scale of this civil war. Many regions face separatist instability. It will take a long and perilous time for Spain to recover, and we must await our next opportunity to close this breach in European security.

options.name: Where Hitler triumphed, we have failed.

title: A Purer Peninsula
desc:
Urgent Dispatch
[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

Reichsminister,

Today is a great day for the Reich; the final outposts of organised resistance against the Spanish National Council have surrendered. Far less timid of the Reich than the preceding junta, already they have offered us a place of honor in the victory festivities being planned, as well as making the return of our diplomatic staff to Madrid a priority. An offer has been expressed for you to attend the parade in person, as well as to the Führer, with President Arrese promising to bestow many honors. The public seem broadly supportive of the Council's proclamations of European fraternity with us, but due to the ongoing instability it is recommended that major visits be postponed.

The nation is in ruins, on a scale not seen in Europe since the Weltkrieg. Cities were already heavily damaged in earlier stages of the fighting, with the fall of the Junta bringing with it renewed destruction. Government authority is firm enough in cities; they are heavily damaged and undergoing continuing stabilization efforts. The countryside remains almost entirely lawless outside of where government military assets are present. I have offered our expertise in stabilising such conditions and contributing to their reconstruction.

The President must still be handled carefully. His duplicitous nature is on record; he may choose a personal path over a path of mutual benefit. A potential replacement is Ramón Serrano Suñer, who enjoys considerable support within the Falange. However, while firmly pro-Germania, he has had a history of difficult personal working relationships with many of the Reich's senior authorities, including Führer Hitler himself. Our victory brings great rewards, there remains possible greater rewards still, but care is still strongly advised.

options.name: A victory surpassing even that of 1939!

title: The Führer's Ulcer
desc:
Urgent Dispatch
[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

Reichsminister,

Despite the hopes that the rise of the National Council would be the first step towards a more prosperous Spain, their final vestiges of organized resistance have surrendered. All embassy staff including myself have been instructed to leave within 48 hours and many volunteers who had been involved with our efforts to rescue Spain from itself have been interred. What remains of Council forces are either surrendering or fleeing towards the French border, with many members of the government already captured or killed. President Arrese is missing, last seen attempting to flee the final National Council's Headquarters with a motorcade.

The scale of the consequences facing the Reich cannot be understated. National Council forces had been in dire need of modernization, training and equipment following the collapse of the Junta. As such their military was given access to Pakt training documentation and supply depots - much of which is now in unfriendly hands. Further, many Germans involved with aiding their forces, from combat volunteers to training officers, have been interred by local forces with fates unknown. Across the Peninsula, our assets are being seized.

It is essential that the Reich collect the remnants of the Falange who can make their escape and create a continuation organization in Germania with which to try and maintain some networks within Spain. Further, diplomatic relations must be reopened with Spain as soon as possible, so as to try and neuter the peninsula as a threat as much as possible from our now-weakened position, as well as to demand the return of interred Germans. Without the abilities such measures would give us, we would be forced to surrender the mouth of the Mediterranean to hostility indefinitely.

options.name: Where Hitler triumphed, we have failed.

title: All Heil the King
desc:
Urgent Dispatch
[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

Reichsminister,

The Kingdom is victorious. The final bastions of the southern usurpers have been expelled from Portugal; King Jaime's throne finally secured from the liberals and socialists who sought to depose him. A letter of thanks has been received from the King, while Foreign Minister Leite has discussed further cooperation. The last vestiges of resistance are being rooted out and the full extent of captured Republicans and foreign interlopers are being assessed.

It must be stressed that the Kingdom remains a somewhat uncertain ally without resolute handling from Germania. Intercepted cables have found Minister Leite is eager to avoid dependence on the Reich, regardless of the necessities of the war, and desires further Mediterranean ties. Lisbon clearly balks at the idea of closer Pakt collaboration, and seeks to establish a relative distance - if a friendly one - now that their need for us is over. The King is little more than a figurehead for now, and much of the government is made up of former Estado Novo members still committed to their ideas of neutrality.

It is absolutely essential all efforts are taken to ensure their wartime promises are followed to completion. Already, Reich assets within the nation are being directed to encourage the Portuguese not to renege upon their promises. Further, the embassy has signalled to the government our willingness to aid further with our expertise in stabilization. Efforts must be undertaken to try and entice the Kingdom away from dalliances with other powers. The potential prize is the Kingdom's hesitancy to move forward being broken, and the Reich gaining a secure Atlantic bastion.

options.name: Europe's most distant outpost is ours.

title: Peninsular Defiance
desc:
Urgent Dispatch
[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

Reichsminister,

The Kingdom to which the Reich had entrusted the repelling of foreign subversion has, as we have feared, failed. Their final bastions of organized resistance have surrendered or been eradicated by republicans. While the exact extent that the Americans and their international thralls will exploit such a victory is unknown, that they are unfriendly to us is clear with little opportunity for rapprochement in the near term. All embassy staff have been given 48 hours to leave the nation.

To be realistic, the alliance with the Kingdom was always one of convenience. Our intelligence made it clear that they worked with us only due to lack of supporters, as such the gains that may have been extracted are somewhat questionable. We can hope that a similar situation is occurring to the Americans, who now will be drawn into the degenerate conflict between the communists and capitalists which bristles in the south. The Estado Novo's doctrines, whose influence lingered even within the Kingdom, has been thoroughly rooted out and Portugal's future is now difficult to predict.

 Training documentation, arms and the numerous volunteers granted to the Kingdom are now in enemy hands. To mitigate this, resolute action is recommended. Lisbon must be pressured to accept a Reich diplomatic presence once again, and the Kriegsmarine must threaten their waters. Atlantic security has been undermined, only a firm hand can preserve what remains. Any dalliance with radical policy threatening Europe must be demonstrated as suicidal. Further briefings can take place upon our arrival to Germania.

options.name: Europe's most distant outpost falls into enemy hands.

title: A Shining Light
desc:
To the Secretary of State,

I am writing personally in light of the resounding success democratic forces have achieved within Portugal. As you have no doubt been prior informed, the Kingdom of Portugal has collapsed and the Republic stands unopposed. President Delgado has publicly thanked Portugal's allies for their assistance, naming the US as chief among them.

Work is now shifting to making the best of this opportunity, as we come to the purpose of this letter. I urge you to impress upon the President the immense importance this victory represents. Already, suggestions are being floated regarding continued American aid as the nation reconstructs, as well as the benefits that OFN assistance may bring in coming years. While the exact extent the Portuguese government will be willing to go in such matters remains to be seen, every opportunity that comes must be seized as we have gained a free, democratic nation on the European mainland.

Further, the President must be made aware of the remaining problems that may yet complicate matters. The Portuguese population remains suspicious of foreign involvement. The new government maintains communist elements who openly push back against further trans-Atlantic collaboration. Further, while Delgado was an opponent of Salazar's, he maintains a personal friendship with the head of the Portuguese Communist Party, Álvaro Cunhal.

 Our victory is substantial, but the President must be aware of the importance of continued vigilance. We have gained a shining light, a burning beacon, to shine into Europe; we can rest assured many will wish to snuff it out.

options.name: U.S. Embassy in Lisbon

title: The General Without Fear
desc:
"What a joke. Guest lecture by Humberto Delgado - the guy's been beaten how many times now?"

"Maybe he'll show us a new ejection technique - got the hell out of Portugal fast enough when things went south."

"Delgado looks... bad. Like he's gonna die at the lectern and save us the trouble."

The shaved-headed Air Force cadets' words, louder than they assumed, about a man, whose English was far better than they assumed, cut through the dry Colorado air to his ears. General Humberto Delgado didn't flinch. He'd heard far worse in recent weeks anyway. The Air Force Academy had invited him here to speak, and that, at least, was something he could still do.

Delgado stepped to the chalkboard and wrote 'Failure'. He waited one, two, three, beats and then began with a growl, "You. If you are men, if you are pilots, you will fail. Missions will go incomplete. Planes will go down. Bro-" his voice choked a little, "brothers-at-arms will die or be mauled until they are unrecognizable. Wars, wars will fail."

"Does that mean the mission should not have been flown? That the plane should not have take off? That the pilot should have never joined the Air Force in the first place? That the war, this century's endless war against fascists and dictators of every stripe, is not worth fighting?"

"No. No, no, and no. But you, they, America, Portugal... will suffer for every failure. I came here today to tell you to be prepared."

options.name: Because I wasn't.

title: Treasure Galleon
desc:
News of the Republic's victory had come over the ship's tinny speakers. As had the order from Washington to proceed anyway with the delivery. The official had said that the food, medical supplies and construction materials were just as welcome as ever. What he hadn't mentioned was that the guns were as well - in the face of localized guerrilla action and an overtly hostile Pakt.

But the supplies would receive a distinctly secondary treatment. Instead, it was the sailors inside that proved the vessel's most precious cargo - for they gave a face to the anonymous American benefactors across the sea in the midst of the most raucous celebration Sevilla had ever seen.

Before the shipping containers had even been cleared from the deck, wine, women, and photographers were flowing in the other direction. Quickly plastered boys from Maryland were soon plastered against the railing by their more haggard counterparts from Malaga or Madrid, each eager to use the few English phrases they had picked up in the war over a bottle. Girls whisked more sober companions away to romantic getaways at the Towers of Gold and Silver or Parque de María Luisa.

Soon, fireworks would illuminate the dusky sky and the Guadalquivir River, highlighting the sailors' awkward but earnest attempts to keep up with their sevillana partners. And two flags, flying side-by-side.

options.name: American by sea, the Republic's by land.

title: Bienvenido... Mr. Marshall
desc:
The Spaniard dragged a wooden chair along the stone floor until it almost touched the bars. But he did not sit. Just lit a cigarette and looked into his prisoner's eyes.

"An indemnity for war widows and orphans. Reconstruction funds for roads and factories. That's what you and your ilk will bring in. You're worth more than your weight in gold, Señor Marshall," his Spanish captor took a long pull from his cigarette as he flipped through the pages of Marshall's passport.

The faint voice from the cell replied, "I'm a civilian contractor. I advise on debt management for J.P. -"

The Spaniard held up the passport to Mr. Marshall's face, "There are only two things I need to know about you, Mr. Marshall. You're an American citizen. And you were in the Republic's'" he spat to the side, "offices when we took Malaga. Truth be told, not even your name matters. I only learned it to be polite."

The Spaniard set down the passport and took another drag of his cigarette before continuing, "And there are only two things you need to know about me. Our European friends have offered a good deal for you. I hope, for your safety, you can convince your government to offer a better one."

The Spaniard took out and started to clean his sidearm, "Because there are more important things than money."

options.name: And my brother died in this war with an American bullet in his head.

title: A Makeshift Embassy Day
desc:
Washington Post - Culture Section

For those new to our fair city, Embassy Day poses an opportunity to partake in the cultural, and, especially, the culinary offerings of the countries formally represented here. Yesterday, Washingtonians experienced Embassy Day in miniature, as diplomatic personnel from the newly-recognized post-Iberian republics opened their doors to the public in celebration of their independence.

These nations, war-ravaged and with scant time in existence, have not yet secured suitably prestigious real estate. But the crowds of well-wishers paid no mind - packing the office building they currently share and spilling out into the street. Several D.C. residents commented on the bravery of their fight for independence against a militarily superior foe, calling parallels to 1776 or expressing support for the U.S.'s armed backing for the republics.

Samples of their national cuisines won over even those unaware of the greater significance of the event. Crema catalana, Galician octopus, and an unpronounceable Basque dish with rabbit appeared the standout favorites, as the quantities prepared ran out before noon.

Satiated residents appeared delighted to welcome the republics to the community of nations, and to their own.

options.name: Independence never tasted so good.

title: Exile Once Again
desc:
"At tonight's meeting of the Council of Galicia, New York chapter, we will be hearing today from the Council's long-time head Antonio Alonso Ríos. As Vice President of the Xunta, Alonso Ríos played an invaluable role in organizing the Galician polity in a time of national emergency. Due to the threats against his life by the occupiers, he and his family have resettled for the time being."

"We are also very pleased to have in attendance tonight three members of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee. Translation services will be provided by Ms. Maruxa Ulloa Peres of the Council of Galicia. Don Alonso Ríos, we're ready for you now."

The balding nationalist took to the microphone, looking a decade older and wearier than the Council had last seen him, "I would like to thank this august body for giving me the opportunity to speak today. And in recognition of our guests, I would like to thank the Senate, and the American people that you represent, for your support in Galicia's darkest hours."

"The Castilian retribution being visited upon the Galician people for daring to dream the dream of independence, of freedom is horrific. Persecution extends beyond those who supported our government, to those who merely express their Galician identity, with intent or merely by our nature. Similar persecution is occurring against our Basque, Catalan, and other neighbors."

"I cannot thank America enough for supporting us in our fight for freedom. No matter how tragic the end of this chapter has been, Galicia will fight on!"

The applause line set hands in motion-

options.name: But in the Senators' eyes, Alonso Ríos saw only pity.

title: Our Boys In Portugal
desc:
FROM THE EMBASSY IN LISBON
ON: [?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]
SECRET—URGENT

It is my pleasure to inform you that stability has returned to Portugal. The Republic has affirmed itself as the sole Portuguese government and the state of civil war can be considered over.

President Delgado has delivered a personal thank you to myself toward the entirety of Brazil, with eager praise for our efforts to support his administration through this difficult period. He gifted a ceremonial wreath, which I have arranged to be sent to your office, and personally addressed a small group of Brazilian volunteer officers and diplomats. He desires to continue our relationship; I feel he will be in need of it. Reconstruction and friends urgently required. I have been informed that Minister of Economy Nuno Simões will propose a trade and investment deal imminently, and not merely from a sense of gratitude. While I cannot yet comment on the extent of cooperation envisaged, Lisbon knows it is in dire need of capital and resources. Due to the near bipartisan support the Republic enjoys in Brazil, in part thanks to the many former exiles who took sanctuary with us, obstructions to our developing relationship are unlikely to develop.

Concerns remain upon minds in Lisbon regarding the communist element within the nation. A necessary alliance during the conflict perhaps, but there are fears that tensions may frustrate between the factions soon. The situation will be monitored, however for the moment such concerns remain merely hypothetical.

Our involvement in Portugal should begin to bear much fruit in the near future. Further developments will be communicated as soon as possible.

options.name: The Atlantic is smaller than ever.

title: Last in Lisbon
desc:
FROM THE EMBASSY IN LISBON
ON: [?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]
SECRET—URGENT

With regret I must inform you of the news we have feared. The state of civil war has ended with the destruction of the Republic of Portugal. The King is soon to arrive in Lisbon and all Brazilian diplomatic and military personnel have been provided 48 hours to leave the nation.

Urgent efforts are being undertaken from our last remaining secure zones near the coast to evacuate. As I write, many personnel and civilians have been safely taken to waiting naval ships or long-range aircraft. Evacuation is frustrated by the many Republican Portuguese nationals also attempting to procure evacuation and sanctuary. In such cases, efforts are being taken to prioritize high-ranking VIPs and their families. Otherwise, this office has ordered that passage must be denied when it is impossible to facilitate.
